a AMES LIAR and Henry Slander are two of VI, best citizens of Dabnque. RED is the natural colour of a young baby, bui

afterwards it becomes a yeller. _ AN electrical girl has been discovered in Cana3a ; she ought to marry a good conductor. SOME moo are so lazy that the " spur of the moment" cannot nociken them into activity. Fuvr people us great a teacher as Jonah. It sagas the whale that brought him up. WHY are a shoemaker's plans always frustrated I .—Because his plans always end in de-feet. PERHAPS one reason why the road of trans gressors is so hard, is because it is so much travelled. 'WHY are some marriages like a circus ? Because they begin with a ring and end with a side throw

A WA6 lent a clergyman a horse that tan away and threw him, and then claimed credit for spread- ing the gospel. WHY was man made with wide-spreading arms, except, as Dryden beautifully supposes, "to satisfy a wide embrace ? ". •
"Is there anything queerer than a queer liues- tion.?" asks an Indiana editor. It strikes us that the qnestioner is the queerist. -
A REVIEWER, in referring to the late Charles Reade's egotism, said—somebody should take pity on his readers, and put out his I's." _ _ _

"MRS. HIGRWATER, how is it I find no cream on your milk ?" Milkman: "Well, mum, I expect the cows are holding it back for strawberry time." "It's as warm as an oven in here," said a citizen as he entered a lawyer's office. So it should be, for it is here I make my bread," said the man of deeds. A COUNTRY PAPER makes the following correc- tion :—" For Its a poor mule that won'twork both ways,' in yesterday's issue, please read, 'lt's a poor rule, &e.' " LADY—" And put just a tint of carmine on the cheeks, but not too much, you know." Photo- grapher—" Exactly, madam—l perfectly under- stand; about as much as you have now." A HUSBAND complains sadly of the price of "ducks." His wife recently bought three for ten guineae—namely, a "duck of a dress, a " duck " of a bonnet, and a " duck " of a parasol. "FATS this I hear y're gaun to dee, Jeannie ? " said an Aberdeen lass to another young woman. " Weel, Maggie, lass, I'm just gaun to marry that farm ower by there, and live wi' the bit mannie "You must not do that, my dear," said a mother to her fonr-year-old daughter. "Nice little girls never do so." "Yes, they do, mamma, some- times ; did'nt you just see me do it 2" was the bright retort. • • •

g'omn singers at a concert were somewhat startled the other evening by finding that the selection, "When wearied wretches sink to sleep," had been printed on the programme, "When mar- ried wretches" &c.
NOTHING makes a woman Eo annoyed as to go to a shoe shop to buy a pair of cheap slippers for her husband and have the shopman try to sell her the identical pair she has just worked for a present for
her minister.

A CETITAIN doctor having heard a village poet repeat some verses on a scolding wife was so delighted with them as to request a copy. "There is no necessity for that," said the poet. " You have got the original." A CHICAGO WOMAN, when asked if she intended to "bring out" her daughter at home, replied, "Oh ! no. I think Washington is a much better place for her to make hec debriq, because the society there is so much more reservo'r than it is in

Chicago." AN ill-humoured woman, abusing her husband for his mercenary disposition, told him that if she was dead he would marry the devil's eldest daughter, if he could get anything by it. "That is true," replied the husband ; "but the worst of it is, I cannot marry two sisters I" A SOCIETY PAPER, in describing the order in which a bridal party passed down the church aisle, says :—" The bride walked on the arm of her father." This may be all right, but it :seems to us that a church was hardly the place for her to dis- play her acrobatic accomplishments. " CHARLI, I'm afraid that if Guzzleby don't stop drinking soon he'll have snakes in his boots," "I'm not." " Why not ?" " Why, there isn't a snake in the world that hasn't more self-respect than to be seen in his company." " Ah, but you know delirium tremens is only an affection of the mind." "Then I'm sure Guzzleby won't have 'ern. 21

THEY were sitting close together on the piazza, when he said: "Georgina, dear, why are you like the moon to-night ?" I don't know, Augustus. Why am I?" "Because there's a circle round you" (lengthening his arm into a joint). " Yes, Augustus; and why are you like the moon ?" "Am I like the moon? Why ? " "Because you are ef- fulgent, Aug4stne." "George, "Ito is your family physician? " Dr. Smootbman." "What, that numbskull? How does happen you employ him?" "Oh, it's some of my lie's doings. She went to see him about a cold itt her head, and he rectrnmended that she wear another style of bonnet. Since that she won't have . .

any other -doctor. ^ A ba4HUI young man could defer the momen- tous question no longer, so he stammered, "Martha, I—l—do you—you must have—are you , aware the Good Book says—er—that it is not g—g ' —gaol that a m—man should be alone?" "Then hadn't you better run home to your mother ?" • coolly suggested Martha. "poop NIGHT, sweetheart, good night," sang a leviA•headed youth as he slammed the front gate an paced paced c-- down the street. Then he took out his handkerchief to rub the rouge off the tip end of his nose, and wondered how much pearl pow- der was a pound when purchased in large quantities. ONCE there was a hired man who was constantly astonishing his employer, a farmer, by doing strange and unexpected things. One day the farmer went into the barn and found the man had hanged himself. Looking at the dangling body a few minutes, he exclaimed; " What on earth will that fellow do next ?" ' ONE day, when Dr.Whately was conversing with a friend, something was said on the subject of re- ligious persecution, on which he remarked, "It is no wonder that some English people have a taste for persecuting on account of religion, since it is the first lesson that most are taught in their nur- series," Ills friend expressed his incredulity, and denied that he, o.t least, had been taught it. "Are you sure ?* replied Dr. Whatcly. "What do you think of ?—" A LOT of unclaimed freight was recently sold at Boston. Among the goods there 'hurled out to be 200 manuscript sermons, written by a Connecticut clergyman. The purchaser discovered curious notes on the margins, such as the following:— " Deliver this passage in solemn tones ;" "Scorn- ful smile after the word ' never ' ;" "Close Bible with violent slam after this passage ;" " Contem- plate ceiling in attitude of adoration at this point;" Sarcastic wave of hand ;" "Rapid gesture. " I i 17,1 very sorry that I did not get acquainted with you until I had become a widower,' said CoL Percy Yerger to his second wife with whom he does not live very happily. "What do you mean by that?" asked the partner of his joys. "Nothing, except, that I would much rather that you had been Toy first wife," replied the fond husband, carelessly. "Why do you wish that 1 had been your first wife "Because some other woman would be my present wife, darling." ThE "funny" man at our club has lately con- tracted the pernicious habit of punning, and the thing is actually getting so bad that we are think- ing of resigning. He always expects only smiles at his jokes, but the other day we really laughed slightly at an ar clot° he told, at which the fellow remarked, " You arc behind time." "Ho, 50?" we asked. "Because your smile is a little after," he replied. NA e rose from the table without a word, and the next morning received by mail a diagram of the joke, as follows :—" A little after—a little laughter." We are happy to say that we are_still able to sign a cheque—for a limited amount. WHEN Dr. Drake heard of a very likely young man staying at Scruton Hall, the residence of some well-apportioned young ladies, he would circulate the report that so-and-so was" b'rutimii" inc."

div.p: " CAPITAL" CHAT.

Mr. Frederick Alers Hankey, M.P., whose death has just been announced, enjoyed a singular reputa• tion in the House of Commons. Although he represented the Chertsey Division of Surrey since 1885, be had not once asked a question, delivered a speech, or moved a resolution. ar

The whole country will be delighted to hear the news that Mr. Herbert Gladstone communicated to the audience in the Foresters' flail, Clerkenwell, on Monday night. He said that when he left Nice last Saturday his father was in the very best of health and spirits, enjoying the sunshine, and ready to face the future.

It is reported in Conservative circles that Minis- ters, having duly .considered the recommendations of the provincial agents of the party who met in London on Saturday, have net been moved from their intention of carrying on the session as long as possible, postponing the dissolution (unless accident intervene) till after the harvest.

Sir Daniel Wilson has bequeathed his brain to posterity. In this he is following the example of Professor Huxley, who, when speaking in the An- thropological section of the Social Science Congress, held in Dublin in 1878, informed the scientists that they were at perfect liberty, after his decease, to make any use of his brain they thought proper. Apropos of Sir Daniel Wilson's recently published book," The Right Hand. Left-handedness, it is in- teresting to know that the caligraph y of Mr. Michael Davitt, who lost his right arm in a manufactory when he was only ten years old, is singularly clear, and indistinguishable, except from its superiority, from the ordinary writing of educated persons who have not met with this affliction. Mr. Davitt is teaching his children to write with both the right and left hands, a custom which is invariably fol- lowed in the schools in the Japanese Empire.

Cypripedium Chamberlainianum is the name given to the new orchid by the gentleman who discovered it in the Merapi Mountains. It is not stated whether the name of the statesman whom Mr. Labouchere has described as" the lap-dog of noble ladies "was given to the new plant because it is a " Lady's Slipper," or because it will net bloom in England.

A correspondent at Florence writes that the news of the Duke of Clarence's death reached that city in a curious manner. Quite a couple of hours before any official or press intimation arrived, an indivi- dual who is concerned in the straw trade entered the club bearing a telegram from London, which ran as follows : "Order hats all black, instead of white, Court mourning."

In conversation with personal friends in the House of Commons on Tuesday night,Lord Randolph Churchill showed himself indisposed to take any active part in the remaining business of the present Parliament. As to what might happen after the General Election he is likely to be guided by cir- cumstances. He does not disguise his conviction that after the general election Mr. Gladstone will return to power by a considerable majority.

Is it not a strange coincidence (asks a Vienna Correspondent) that Tuesday, the very day when the opera " Werther " was performed for the first time, a grandson of the heroine Lotte, Herr Georg Kestner, should have shot himself with a pistol in the head, so that he died on the spot? He committed the act while delirious in consequence of influenza. He was born in 1803, and was therefore 87 years

Colonel Olcott, who was Madame Blavatsky's partner in the founding of the Theosophical Society, and has been its piesident from the begin- ning, has signified his intention of retiring from that giddy height of dignity. Whether he is about to qualify for mahatmasbip tidings tell not ; but as he is a nice, stout, gentle-looking old man, with a long venerable white beard and white hair, he really ought to be a mahatma. He is at present in India.

Rumour was never more astray than when it said that Mr. Algernon Tollemache had left most of his fortune to the Duke of Teek. The Duke's name was not mentioned in the will,although Mr. Tollemache had £1,2t37,000 to give away. This includes a great New Zealand estate, where there is no distinction between realty and personalty. The personal estate in England was £814,235, 66 that the probate duty paid would be £24,426. Lord Sudeley's wife bene- fits chiefly under the will. Lady Sudeley was rich before, and will now be one of the wealthiest women in England.

Mr. Tollemache was the last brother of the eccen- tric Earl of Dysart, who shut himself up for thirty years in 34, Norfolk-st., Strand. That old peer was a professed hater of women. No maid dared enter his presence. He ate and drank alone, and stories were even told of his dinner being pushed through a hole in the wall. He had a Bluebeard chamber, where he kept his title deeds, and it was his only amusement to shut himself up and inspect them. This was said to have suggested to Dickens the idea of the old lady who kept her wedding break- fast under lock and key,and visited it every day un- til she died. The old Earl left £1,700,00P, most of it to the present peer and his sisters. Mrs.Tollemache- Scott, of Bosworth Park, and Lady Westbury.

The French Parliament having spent last year in passing a Protectionist Act, will evidently have to occupy its time this year in rescinding its more baneful clauses. At the first sitting of the Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday, a proposal was made to fix a minimum wage for workmen in consequence of the increased price of food under the new tariff. It has only been in force two weeks, and already the price of all necessaries of life has risen. The French Government in introducing Mliinleyism was acting in the interests of manufacturers and the landlords. If the Act is allowed to work its worst for a year or two, France will be saved from the mischievous action of Protectionists in the future.

Dr. Perry, the late Anglican Bishop of Melbourne, succeeded in scraping together the tidy little total of £33,518—a figure which is in somewhat sharp contrast to Cardinal Manning's £l5O. He arrived in Australia three years before the gold discoveries of 1851, and returned to England in 1874. Clergy- men who officiated on the goldfields for the first few feverish exciting years were usually in luck's way. Thus Dr. Backhaus,the Roman Catholic Dean of Bendigo, died worth £300,000. But he was a doctor in a double sense—a medical man and an ordained priest who had taken the degree of D.D. He cured both the spiritual and corporal ailments of the diggers, and was rewarded with nuggets of gold.

Dr. Henry Allon's colleague in the pastorate of Union Chapel. Islington, who began his ministry on Sunday—the Rev. W. 11. Harwood—is a man whose splendid physical proportions would alone suffice to render him a notable figure in the ranks of metro- politan Congregational divines. But he has other I elements of power ; readiness of utterance, a clean- cut and incisive rhetoric, fervour of declamation, and a suggestive and masterful gesture. He brings the fine free spirit of the north to London. His nine years pastorate at Villiers-st. Chapel, Sunderland, which has just terminated, has been an eminently successful one. His profound sympathy with the masses, and his catholicity in the domain of reli- gious creed, mark him out distinctly as a suitable co-pastor and eventual successor of the Nestor of English Congregationalism.

div.head: CALCULATING PRODIGY.
div.p: A CALCULATING PRODIGY.

Inaudi, the calculating prodigy, was subjected to some severe tests on Saturaay in the Sorbonne, before an audience composed of professors and pupils of all the Paris Lsc(les. Both teachers and students put abstruse arithmetical problems before him; but Inaudi never faltered, effecting multipli- cations and divisions of sums containing 24 figures, und extracting square and cube roots with 17 deci- mal places in an astoundingly rapid manner. After having finished these calculations, Inaudi carefully repeated on the blackboard all the figures which he had mentally operated upon without having seen them. It is noteworthy (the "Daily Telegraph's" correspondent says) that the young man's faculties are slow as regards everything not connected with arithmetical or algebraic quantities. Thus he reads and writes only indifferently well, and stated that he could not commit to memory the shortest ex- tract from a literary work. Inaudi is simply a cal- culating machine, and nothing more.

Whitaker's Almanack for 1892, has been con- siderably enlarged in some of its sections, the editor watching the signs of the times and taking care to give valuable information upon those sub- jects which are prominently before the public. No little space is therefore devoted to educational mat- ters, and there is a separate article on educational progress during recent years, besides a record of the principal occurrences of the past year. There is too,a special article on agricultural education. There is a general review of the progress of Methodism given in connection with details of the Wesleyan centenary. Amongst papers which appear for the first time are those on naval gunnery ; and, most important of all, the result of the late census. The labour involved in producing such an exhaustive volume is enormous, for, as the editor remarks, " every page and almost every line of the work has been corrected, and, as early as possible, brought up to the date of issue. In many instances the changes wrought during the brief interval of a sin- gle year are so numerous that scarcely a line of the section in which the subject is dealt with, remains unaltered." The almanack, in addition to giving an account of astronomical and other phenomena, fur- nishes a laige amount of information respecting the Government finances, population, commerce, and general statistics of the British Empire throughout the world.

"Stories from the Bible" (2nd series) is from the pen of the Rev. Alfred J. Church, with illustrations after Julius Schnorr. These stories are simply and beauti- fully written with an eye to finding a ready entrance into the minds of children, and at the same time great care has been taken to ensure that everything stated shall be as accurate as it is interesting. Notes are given at the foot of the pages, with a view 'to furnishing such explanations as may be deemed necessary. The illustra- tions, it should be mentioned, are of altogether a supe- rior kind. The contents of this volume include amongst others, the stories of Esau, Jacob, Samson, Samuel, Solo- mon, Abraham, Elijah, Elisha, and Daniel. Messrs. Macmillan and Co. are the publishers, and the work is admirably printed and handsomely bound. The issue to hand of "The Golden Treasury" series, published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., is "The fairy book; the best popular stories selected and rendered anew" by the author of "John Halifax Gentleman." It is evident from reading these stories that Mrs. Craik's labour has been a labour of love. She has travelled the world over, so to speak, to obtain the best stories from every country, and it is a matter of course to say that she has omitted none of tho real old English fairy tales, such as "Tom Thumb," "Jack the Giant Killer," &c. Referring to the fairy tales of other countries, Mrs. Craik says " Where it was not possible to get at the original of a tale, its various versions have been col- lected, compared, and combined, and in some instances where this has still proved unsatisfactory, the whole story has been written afresh." It will be seen, therefore, . that this volume is unique in its way, and as it contains close upon 40 fairy tales, it will be a permanent source of delight to all the little folk who have the good fortune to secure a copy. The " English Illustrated Magazine" for February has for frontispiece a remarkably fine portrait of Mr. Arthur Balfour, the new leader of the House of Commons, followed by a brief biographical sketch from the pen of Mr. H. W. Lucy. Considerable spacs is devoted to a profusely illustrated article on " The London and North Weston Locomotive Works at Crewe." It may be said to be authoritative, for it is written by C. J. B. Cooke, assistant running superintendent to the locomotive department. Other illustrated papers, &c., are" Brahan Castle," " How pianos are made," "Mrs. Humphry Ward," " Mosques of Tlemcen," and "The girl of the period." " For Light and Liberty" is the title of the latest story by the Rev. Silas K. Hocking, author of " Her Benny,' "Real grit," &c. It is having a large circulation, appealing as it does, to the religious world,in showing up the weak side of scepticism in the person of Phillip Hardman. It seems to us that the author has overdone the part, and shows that he himself is not without strong prejudice in these matters. Still, there is a good deal of pleasant reading in the volume, and no little variety, the character of the boy Eric being very well drawn. The price of the story is 2s. 6d., and it is published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co. . _ .

"The Westminster Review " for February treas at number of important topics with characteristic strength and clearness, and Mr. J. A. Newton-Robinson contri- butes a pleasing study of Mr. Thomas Hardy as a novelist. Lord Rosebery's " Pitt" is ably reviewed by Mr. R. Seymour Long, and other subjects are dealt with as follows :—" Bibliolatry," by the Rev. Walter Lloyd, Savonarolo in history and fiction," by the Rev. J. Jessop Teague, "China : a far eastern question," by Mr. W. Robertson," A teaching University for London," by Mr. J. Spencer Hill, and" Is compulsory education a failure 2" by Mr. J. J. Davies. The frontispiece of the current issue for the " Cen- tury," magazine is a reproduction of Titien's "La Bella." There is a second paper, illustrated, on "The Jews of New York." and a striking illustrated article on " Pioneer days in San Francisco." Titien is dealt with in the continued series of papers on "Italian old mas- ters." A further account is given of the original portraits of Washington and Nelly Custis. There is a good supply of continued and completed fiction, and of open letters and " Verse in lighter vein," the number being an alto- gether strong one. In the " Newbery House Magazine" Dr. Hayman re- plies with characteristic vigour to Professor Goldwin Smith's remarks on disestablishment. The biographical sketch of Sydney Smith is concluded, and very pleasant reading it proves. The Rev. Canon Carter has an article on" The intercession of Christ," and there is as exceedingly readable paper on "Church folk lore," by the Rev. J. E. Vaux,confirming what Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, said the other day about there being a lire in one of the pews of the old Parish Church of War- rington. The writer says that "pews had been sometimes filled with sofas and tables, and even provided with fireplaces." He quotes Mr. Abbey as saying that "cases might be mentioned where the tedium of a long service or the appetite engendered by it were relieved by the entry between prayers and sermon of a liveried servant with sherry and light refreshments." Amongst the illustrated articles, &c., in. the "Ladies' Treasury" are "Italy and its fortunes," "'Curious trees,"" Descriptions of needlework," "Notes on the fashions," and •• The death of the Duke of Clarence." The stories and sketches, &c., are as usual, interesting and well-written.

" AKey to Farriery • or veterinary practice at home," published by Messrs. Day, Son'- and Hewitt, is having a large run' having reached a 14th edition. The work certainly deserves to be popular, for it is admirably pre- pared, with a view to giving valuable information on a great variety of topics, and in very small space. The object of the work is to enable stock owners to employ rational and ready means of cure in all cases of emer- gency and simple ailments. No person who has to do with horses, cattle, sheep, or pigs, should be without a copy of this work. Messrs. Day, Son, and Hewitt deal with these matters from practical knowledge, as they are the sole proprietors and manufacturers of " The chemical extract," " Gaseous fluid," " Red drench," "Bed paste," " Broncholine," " Gaseodyne," , We have also to hand Weldon's "Ladies' Journal of Dress,Fashion, and Needlework " (3d.), and lers.Leach's "Family Dressmaker" (2d.), "A Guide to Home Dress- making," and "Practical Advice to Housewives." We have received the first number of "The Story of Africa and its Explorers," which is being issued by Messrs. Cassell and Co., in monthly parts at 7d. each. With part one there is presented a large map of Africa, hardsomely printed in colours, showing the routes of ' the principal explorers and European possessions and spheres of influence. As the work is written by Dr. Robt. Brown, M.A., himself an experienced traveller, it is hardly necessary to say that it will be exceedingly in- teresting, especially as the text will be accompanied by illustrations of the highest class.

div.p: --o-- REMARKABLE BRA.ITERIf OF A SAILOR

The Prince Edward's Island schooner Avenger has been driven on the rocks twenty miles from St. John's N.F., the wreck being characterized by a re- markable exhibition both of bravery and strength. The schooner was pounding to pieces in the tremen- dous surf, and the single boat was swamped in an effort to launch it, Then Murdoch Gillis, a sailor, offered to swim ashore with a life line, and jumped overboard. He was thrown on the rocks by a big wave, but was unable to obtain a hold, and after being bruised, tossed, and buffeted was hauled back. He rested an hour, and then tried again. This time be was thrown into a cleft in the face of a cliff, from which he climbed point by point!until he obtained good holding ground. He then drew ashore and 'fastened a larger line, by which the captain and all the crew were saved.

CHAPTER XIV. WILATING THE PRESS oANW,'-,'

Now at last the news was out, and terrible news It proved to all there. Little by little Bell nl4tuAged to gather the exact facts of the case. , • A. recruiting brig had been lying off shore all day, but no sign of a landing from it had been seen, and little notice was, therefp,m,paid to its presence. Vter Bill Widdrington had spent an hour or so with his sweetheart, he had gone out and met with some of his acquaintances among the fishermen. After exchanging a few words, the whole party— some half-dozen or so, all big, stalwart tritons— had adjourned to the "Fisherman's Rest," a little public-house kept by Bessie Carr, Ailsie's aunt, with the intention of having a friendly glass together. No sooner had they grown merry over their grog than a startling interruption to the harmony of the evening took place. A small boy of ten years of age, son of Bessie Carr, came rushing in, breathless with excitement. " Ye're dynne for non, every one o' ye," he cried, half sorrowful, and yet swelling with the import- ance of his knowledge, "the chaps fra' the brig's landed, an' they're close ahint me ; ye'll ha' to serve the King noo 'stead o' mindin' yer boats." The warning was too late to be of much service. The boat's crew were close at the heels of the bearer of ill tidings. Deep and loud resounded the cprses of the fishermen. They were trapped like rats in a hole. They determined, however, to fight in defence of their liberty. In the twinkling of an eye every door and win- dow was closed and barred; tables and chairs were piled up against them- to form a hasty barricade, and pokers, knives, axes, with everything else at all available as a weapon of defence, were seized upon. The hostess and her handmaidens, trembling and dismayed, hid themselves in closets and under bedsteads. 1.2 there was to be a serttranage they thought it better to be discreet and keep out of it. Besides, when such dangerous weapons were brandished who could tell where a danger might menace? After the preparation were completed a few moments of suspense ensued. Every ear was strained to catch the first sound of feet, the demand for entry in the name of the King. No answer was made to the first summons, but when a second fellowed close upon it the men there assembled gave a shout of derision simul- taneougy— , '4Ol Tar ways back where ye come shouted Bill Widdrington, in a clear voice, "we'll fight ,ye' afore we fight the froggies, ma canny Lads

There was a consultation outside, and then the officer in command produced his pistol, and with great deliberation placed it against the lock. "If thy will not open we Must e'en force it," he said griffily, and fired, thereby shattering the clumsy lock to .toms, and wounding one of the besieged, who was, unfortunately, stooping down to examine its capabilities at the time of the explo- sion. After this there was little chance for the clumsy barricades to hold back the enemy. A rush of sailors against the door burst it open, and sent the tables and chairs flying all over the place. Then, with cutlasses drawn ready for the fray, the press gang entered, and the battle began. But what chance had the poor fishermen against their opponents? It was all over in a few minutes. The resistance was a brave one, but could not be successful against numbers and skilled fighters. Soon were they overborne, and now lay panting and exhausted in durance vile. They were to stay there until morn- ing, and then be removed to the tender. All this Ailsie told to Bell with many sighs and tears to interrupt the narrative. "Oh, Bell, hinny, we'll never, never see his bonny face again. Awm' sure he'll be killed in the war, because aw love him so, an' aw canna' live without him."
" Eigh, weigh, there's more unlikely things than come to pass!' was Nanny's consolatory remark. Although the. news moved her to sorrow, she _ .
was still touchy because Bell had refused to acknow- ledge her great powers of prophecy, and to accept her ill-omened dreams as final.

"Much. you seem to mind !" cried little Ailsie, turning upon the old woman with fierce eager. "You're a Job's comforter to be sure. If one was to listen to you, there'ud be nothing but evil to look forward to in this life. As if it was na' bad enough to lose ma' canny lad, oh marcy me; as if that wasn't enough !" and covering her face with her apron the little creature sobbed afresh. Then she made another appeaL "Oh, Bell, woman, canna' ye think of owt to comfort me. Just to lose him at this time, when—when we were preparin' for the weddin' an' aIL Aw'll gan clean daft if aw canna' get a bit o' hope. Aw'll drown mysel' an' be dynne with it, aw warn ye that !" Whist thee noo' lass, and let me alone. Aw'm thiakin', an' canna' be fashed wi' talk." The strong.nature shook off the weak, while it communed with itself as to what was to be done, not being content to own the mischief as inevitable. After a little a light came into Bell's eyes, and the raised her head proudly. "Ye skull has yer man back again, little one I Aw'nt off noo to fetch him—only ye'll ha' to be content to know he's safe, and to let him be oot sight for a bit I" But how, Bell? What are ye gannin' to do t" Bell gave a merry laugh.- - " Cheat the devils—that's what aw'in gannin' to do !"

lifot a moment was to be lost, and tying a shawl over her head, Bell ran down the road to the village of Breamish. The prisoners were bolted and barred into a room, with two of the press gang keeping guard over them. Upon this scene entered Bell, crying piteously, and entreating to be allowed to see her brother, were it only to say farewell. . "No, no, my lass, our orders are strict, that no one is to be admitted," declared one sailor, fortify- ing himself against a suspicious softening .of the heart, by an extra severity of speech and aspect. "Eli, me, what harm can aw do them ?" asked Bell, innocently, "if ye were bein' taken off like that, without a minute's notice, and leavin' an old grandmother and me to get oor livins', wadn't ye Ike a minute to talk o' ways and means ?" The girl's eyes looked so wistful, and so utterly devoid of guile, that the man wavered. He looked at his comrade in arms doubtfully. Now the other and younger seaman was of an exceedingly inflammable nature, like most of MS class, for Jaok, with whom familiarity has no chance of breeding contempt has ever a warm side for the sex, and he was regarding Bell's lovely face and fine proportions with undisguised admiration. "I'm blowed if You are not the finest lass I've set eyes on for more than a twelvemonth," he ex- claimed enthusiastically, "and only to think haw it's likely enough that ye'll be thrown away on some land-lubber or other, when his Majesty's Navy has so little time to court suitable wives and beget fine families! One question you'll allow me: 'Have you a sweet heart, my dear?' I don't mean no rudeness, but only a respectful enquiry with an object in view?" "Sweetheart, indeed !" repeated Bell, with in- dignation; then remembering her conciliatory tac- tics' she gave him a demure glance, from under her long eyelashes, "And how is a poor maid to hey a chance of a sweetheart, let alone s. good man, when ye take away all wor best-lookin' lads, and never send them back to us, except only when they've lost thew arms or legs? An' though we dinna shew them that we mind, an' made shift to do the best we can wi' the poor cripples, it isn't to be expected that any lass should be content•vii' half a man if she could get a whole 'un ?" "Certainly not! Least of all such a beauty as you," assented the sailor, laughing at her naivet. "Well, I've been in a battle or two, but can boast of all my members yet, thank heaven! and only a French bullet, somewhere about my ribs, that bothers me a bit at times, but generally behaves itself peacable to distinguish me from those who have never been in action ! If so be as you're not bespoke, and could look with a favouring eye upon me, I would come to these parts, when leisure allows, and make you a true and loving husband; and bring you all my prize money into the bargain." " Darrsay ! Au' a sweetheart in every port, and may be a wife and bairns waitin' on ye doon sooth !" " What ? A true tar mislead a sweet young lass But ye don't mean a word of it." "Ma poor Bill inside there's gettin' a sweet-heart though, and aw' promised her aw'd gie' him her message, for she's fair heart-broken! " "Has she sent him anything else eh, my dear? kiss, for instance ? " ailheA the amorous tar;

ant Ind Dell's waist, he id to & vaned without his host, ever, ing herself free, she admiiiis', ed to him a sounding box on the ear, that made it tingle for half an hour afterwards, His comrade roared with laughter at his discom- fiture, and applauded the strength and courage of the North-country lass. "That'll teach ye manners, Dick Jackson," he said, in high glee, "ye might ha' seen with half an eye that this was -no light-minded jade, ready to take on with every blue jacket she came across; but a decent, sensible girl, such as I hope my own little 'un at home will be when she comes to the same age!" " What ! Ye have bairns o' your own, canny man, and yet ye're so hard on me for just wantin one little cuddle and kiss o' my own brother, the brother that aw' may never, never see more, once he gans' wi' ye? 04, ,do let me have one look at him? Aw'll promise not to stop many minutes, and ye can bolt and bar me in all the time along with him—there now. Oh, ye dear kind aad man, aw' knew ye were the best o'. the two fro' the first!"

And rather to the elder man's embarrassment, she put her arms round his .neck and voluntarily gave him the kiss she had denied to his comrade. After all this-courting the.old man proved pliable, and reflecting probably that nothing very serious could happen while the prisoners were under lock and key, he admitted the girl, locking her in, and cautioning her not to stay long. Sulky and despairing, the three fishermen who had been impressed sat there in the darkening room, thinking of their wives and sweethearts. Bill was in a kind of stupor, for he was wounded slightly and had lost blood, though his arm had , since then been properly bandaged by the doctor. , Bell went to him, and shook him. "Come Bill, lad, there's not a minute to lose We've come to cheat the devils, and to set thee free." _ _ _

"Set me free? But how ? " asked Bill with little hope, even in Bell, who was always reckoned the cleverest in the family. " Dinna ask questions, but obey orders! off wi' yer coat, lad. jack Stokoe and Davy Taylor gan ower to the other side o' the room yonder, and turn yer heids to the wall, and look round at yer peril—aw'm garn to change my claes !" The men grasped hr idea immediately, and ol)ey-ed with chuckles of delight at her quick wittedness. Poor fellows, it was hard on them that there was not one to do the like good office for them. But there is a lot of esprit de corps about these people, and they did not grudge a com- rade better luck. " Yell have to hide i' th' cave ye know on, Bill, but Ailsie look after ye- She knows all about it. Make straight for the hidin' hole, who knows how soon they may find me oot ?" " But Bell, hinny, aw divvent like leavin' thee? What'll thee, when they discover it?" "Dear knows Make a man-o'-war's man o' me, ' may be, if aw'll fight. Atr win' 1-?(? thjii first woman that's dune that, by all accOunig I Hoots, lad, they'll de me ne hort, anyway I There, too, lint the shawl over thy held, and dinna take lang strides and be sure and pipe yer eye, as ye gan oot, and ye'd take in Cranny, let alone the King's men ! Ire're the very image o' me, as everybody kens !" _ _

When the door opened, and the stalwart fisher lass came slowly out, and sobbed and held her shawl up to her face, the kindly old tar, whose sympathies she had won, clapped her on the shoulder, and bade her take comfort, for that her canny brother should come back to her safe and sound, and not with both his legs shot away. But it was so dark that he noticed nothing amiss, and the visitor went off, but slowly, to avoid any sus- picion of haste. The other and sharper sighted of the guards was too sore about the way in which his love-making had been received to risk another en- counter, so avoided even looking at the one who had so worsted him. Great was the wrath of the gang when they discovered how they had been duped ; but what could they do? There was no redress. True, Bell declared her willingness to serve his Majesty in the place of her twin brother, but such an offer was considered to be adding in- sult to injury! They scoured the country in search of the defaulter; but as the prejudices of the natives were all against them, and as there was no manner of doubt the said natives were all ready to aid and abet the young fisherman in his es- cape, and as, moreover, the vicinity abounded in caves and secret places known only to those en- gaged in free trading, there was small chance of his recapture, and after a time the sailors recog- nised this, and wasted no more days in the search. To add to their chagrin they became objects for the scorn and derision of the fishing population. Laughter and mockery resounded from all sides when they paraded the village. "Where's the lass that ye're gaun to mak a sailor on? They maun be easy to lick, them Frog,gies, sin the women-folk hey to be pressed te fight. Man alive! To think such blivvor cheps should be bamboozled by a lass !" - Such were the jeers of the women and children. At that time, and during its occupation by the navy, the village boasted few male residents save such as age and infirmity rendered of no avail for fighting purposes. There was nothing left for his Majesty's Navy but to allow Bell to go, and retreat themselves with what grace they could muster. Their humiliation was great at being outwitted by a woman, but there was no redress possible.
CHAPTER XV . A PARTI-COLOURED ROSE.

/glen summer came, Lady Callerley was completely reconciled to her home and its sur- roundings. The sea—forgetting its erstwhile wrathful moods —went murmuring along the far reaching stretches of sand in soft soothing lullabies. Grey and sullen no longer, wonderful sapphires and emeralds from the brilliant sunshine were caught and flashed back from its rippling surface or it lay, languid and spell bound, wider the level rays of sunset, soft tender opaline tints suffusing it. Then too, every sullen rock and craggy head- land was bathed in dreamy golden mists. At this season even the ugly, level, monotonous sand-hills caught some grace froni bounteous nature.

An undergrowth of wild thyme, yellow crows- foot, and pink and purple thrift, sprang up and diversified charmingly their scanty herbage. The cold greyness of the coarse bent grass was broken and varied also by greener tints. Life, fresh, vivid life, awoke everywhere. The white wings of gulls flashed in the sunshine; sea swallows twittered amongst the stones; merry little birds, dotterils and sand pipers, ran along the sand or busied themselves amid the heaps of wreck and seaweed; while overhead, skylarks shrilled out their rapture continuously. The very sand hoppers and the shrimps added to the feel- ing of joyousness, by their quick movements and friskiness.
SOIM

It was good to be alive in those days, and Silvia felt it so! Jack Breamish was often her companion, when Sir Lancelot was too busy or too pre-occupied to have rambles down to the shore, or up by the burns. Time hung heavily on hand with the young fellow, and he was always ready to be Silvia's escort. Sir Lancelot thought it natural enough that his girl wife should sometimes wish for younger and brighter society than his own though the slight feeling of pique and envy which had first sprung to life at first sight of Jack and Silvia together, both so pleasant to look upon, and so eminently well matched in youth and joyousness, came back, ever and anon, to sting the grave gentleman with painful force. But Jack's frankness and simplicity had won upon him, and his own nature was as yet too generous to harbour envy, still less jealousy—had it been let alone, that is; but withal, the nature inherited by him was a suspicious one, if once set ageing on a course of doubt, and there were in it capabilities of savage jealously and violent hatred, knowirand reckoned upon by one person, too surely for his peace of mind in the future. The story of young Breamish's smart coat had amused Sir Lancelot, and touched him a little too, when the squire told it, in his blunt way, as an after dinner joke at his brother's expense. "By Jupiter, sir! If the young fool didn't sell the only horse he possessed, a roan with a star, that I'd offered him my brown mare and twenty pounds into the bargain for, two months pre- viously, when I was in cash—sold it at a dead loss, so to speak, for ready-money to buy a fine suit in ' which to visit thy little bride! not that I quarrel with the youngster for trying to keep up the family credit, but to cut a dash not a crown piece to keep the pocket of his plum ,coloured coat,--,-ha, ha, its as good as a farce, it is, by Venus I." "How conies it that a fine young fellow like your brother should be left to rust in a country place, while his Majesty wants men to fight for him on land and sea?" asked Sir Lancelot. The Squire's thick..exebrowa, contracted, and hie face grew redder than ever. . . .
" Damme, sir, whose fault is that?' he burst out vehemently. "when a man's married hp can't do as

money is short, and there'si- a young up and educate, and—and by lerley, I don't know which way to turn iies; and a young man of family cannot enlist as a common soldier, as the lad would fain do! But when I have a turn of luck, tbe youngster shall 'share it, I give you my wad for that." "Poor Jack!" "Oh, the beggar's happy enough with his fishing, and a bit of shooting I give him now and again when the birds get over thick, and now your pretty Lady Callerley has taken him up—which is a spoke in Madam's wheel, by Vulcan! and I'm not sorry for it, I can tell you—well, since he has gone so much to Seaton Callerley, I say he is quite content, and would'nt call the King his cousin ? " "But his coat will grow shabby by and by, and he'll feel ashamed to come to Seaton Callerley. How about his contentment then?" "Let him alone for managing to get a new one. Don't bother about the lad. He'll come on all right, as sure as God made little apples! If Madam would only wink sometimes, one might have a chance of helping him," the. hitt man said in a whisper, which showed very plainly which way the wind New.

Sir Lancelot felt contemptuous as he noted what he called the poltroonery of the burly man. What on earth was there in his soft spoken cousin to in- spire such abject dread? She only needed once to acknowledge a master, to be all that was desirable in a wife. He could not understand Only the henpecked can fully understand and sympathise with those in like condition. The man who, when driving had the right of precedence, gave in quite amicably to the other whose spouse, seated alongside, claimed it unjustly and with feminine vigour of language: "Gan on forst, hinny, and welcome! Aw've a match for thee at home, and aw never crosses her without catchin' it het wi' th' rough edge o' her tongue Aw's sorry for thy canny man, so take thy own way!" This was practical sympathy, and as such surely deserves honourable mention. The Squire might bluster, and rage, and swear by all the heathen gods and goddesses as much as he chose (the reason he chose these names to em- bellish his conversation, was not because he was well up in Greek mythology and wished to show it, but because these were the names of his favourite dogs), but in all weighty matters, Madam ruled the roost. In some respects this was greatly to his advantage, for she certainly possessed a clever business head, and had not his affairs been too in- extricably involved when he married, she might possibly have pulled him through. Sir Lancelot respected the secret of the coat. He guessed that Jack's pride would be sadly hurt if it were known, ant kept silence accordingly. He else Negate up his mind that at the first oppor- tunity that presented itself, he would give the lad tshelsiing hand. But it must be done in such a way " that Lel: would not know the source from which the favour—whether in the form of eommission or otherwise—carae, for Sir Lancelot was sufficiently setsitive himself to understand and appreciate the pride of a poor gentleman. He bad small faith in the Squire's turn of luck ; Jack might live on an aimless life to old age ere that daMit Lady CalleSless, whose sympathies were on the side of love rather than of law, was delighted when she heard of Bell Widdrington's exploit with the press-gang; and pretty helpless Ailsie won her heart by outspoken joy ard delight in the recovered treasure; who, after skulking about for weeks amongst the caves used by the free-traders for the stowage of their goods, and being petted and made much of by his womankind, after the manner of the sex, ventured, when the coast was clear, to return to his home no end of a hero in his own estimation. He had not done anything very wonderful, to be sure, and what praise was forthcoming was cer- tainly due to his sister. But Bell laughed off any idea of heroism, and grew tired of the subject very speedily, so her twin had it all to himself, and a trifle of rheumatism contracted during his enforced seclusion in damp underground places, was magni- fied into a serious complaint, which required to be treated to many glasses of whisky by sympathising admirers, before it was thoroughly washed out of the system. Only the stern and hard natured Cuddy confided to his pious widow his firm convic- tion that the young one was " foxing " in order to shirk his just share of work, and to be made a fool of by the women. Whereupon .finny Dodd, Matthew Ogle's widow woman, held up her hands In righteous horror at such wicked and hypocritical doings, and prophesied, rather inappropriately, the fate of Ananias and Sapphire on the profane young ruan who dared to invoke a judgment, by aspiring to a disease he did not possess. The pious widow had a consciousness that Bill, with his everlasting love of joking, poked fun at her, and this did not tend to render her more lenient to his feelings. She was more sensitive to ridicule than such a professed saint ought to have been, Lady Gallerley's views coincided entirely with those of pretty Ailsie, who was exceedingly afraid of the cup slipping again when near her ready lips, and decided that the sooner Bill and she were made one, the better. Although the King's recruiting men did not take the trouble of discriminating between married and single, she would at least make sure of the time before they made a cripple or a wooden legged man of her sweetheart. Old Nanny Widdrington did not enjoy the pros- pect of the wedding, -because, besides being her favourite, he was main contributor to the little luxuries which at her time of life are so much more than any mere necessaries ; and she was afraid that matrimony might cause forgetfulness of these to ensue. She took to dreaming hard, and interpret- ing her dreams; most dismally; but Dill only laughed, and Ailsie grew cross. Bell, on the contrary, thought marriage would steady the lad, and therefore encouraged the

- notion. When it was settled, she came to Seaton Callerley to inform Silvia of the day fixed for the ceremony • as besides her interest in the young couple, Lady Callerley had expressed a wish to be present at a fisher wedding. When her news was communicated, the fisher lass lingered, as though loth to depart. Silvia, who admired the girl, and was growing very fond of her, noticed this, and wondered a little. "You have something more to say, Bell! Surely you are not afraid of me?" Still Bell did not speak. She looked very beautiful as she stood there, hesitating and shy, the evening light playing round her golden hair, and bringing out the rich tints on her complexion. "What is it, child ?" asked the little lady kindly. It was nice to be able to condescend and encourage a grand creature like this. "Bell, how splendid your hair is in this sunset light, and how I wish I were tall and strong, and handsome like you. There, you need not blush so, everybody knows I don't stop to think before I speak! But come, tell me what it is that bothers you." "It's nowt to mention mebbe, and yet aw felt as though there were mititChief th' air, when I seed and heard it! An' ye've been kind to all on us, and th' smile o' yer bonny bit mouth, and th' joke always ready, so hoo can aw hand my tongue Jhen a word o' warnin' might do good? This is hoo it was! Aw had to gang up to th' Hall wi' some stockin's granny had been knittin' for Master Lancey, and aw was waitin' on Madam in her own sittin' room, when who should come close up to the window outside but Madam hersel' and young Jack—that is Mr. Jack Breamish, ye know! She's not very fair spoken to him most times, but lust then she had on her soft manner, mindin' me for all the world of a cat, as it turns a mouse ower and owcr wi' its eushiony paws that ye wadn't guess had such tarrible prongs hid i' them, as she tapped aim on th' arm with her fan, playful like! The window was open at th' top and aw' could hear quite fair what they were talking about. "'So ge've been at Seaton Callerley as usual," she said, looking at him sideways wi' them cowld glittering eyes o' hers, an' was cousin Lancelot there, or only cousin Silvia?' "Aw couldn't hear what Mr. Jack answered, but it evidently amused Madam, for she laughed out loud. "'What a pretty rose you are wearing, Jack? I only know one place where those roses grow. Is it. a cousinly favour?' "Mr. Breamish looked black as thunder in a moment, and crumpling the rose up in his hand, threw it away. He turned on his heel, and was hastening off, when a sudden thought seemed to strike him, and he went back and faced her. " I stole the rose, Madam, if it is any satisfac- tion to you to know how I became the possessor of it !" he said quickly, and then left her alone there. She stood for a minute or two longer, an' aw could see she was thinkin' hard. Then she laughed again, and it was such a wicked kind o' laugh that , cuddent bide to hear it. Her hands kept grippin' themselves together, like she was eliok somebody. Neebody lives that isn't frightened o' Madam when her temper's roused. But site kind o' kept it under this time, though aw could see it was smoulderin'. " Aw'll spoil the sport if aw cannot hand my tongue fra' jeerin' him,' she said to herscl' softly, b.ut_aw...had am& closer and aw qc021(1 hear her

"She passed on when she said this, and aw knew that if she catched me there'd be a fine shindy, so aw managed to get the window shut and creep away to the far side o' th' room, afore she found aw was there; and when she came in there was nowt to show aw'd seen or heard anything. j3ut cm felt ye ought to know she's hatchin' misShiefe an' aw hope, ma leddy, ye'll not be vexed wi me for tale bath'?" "What sort of rose was it that Mr. Bream'sh wore?" asked Lady Callerley. This conversation took place in her sitting-reern, and the window was open that looked into the Dutch garden. There a profusion of roses bloomed, good, old-fashioned, sweet-scented comely roses, which did not scruple to grow luxuriantly and to flower abundantly; maiden's blush, damask, Pure white and pink, and that small yellow rose with a delicious fragrance which is now almost extinct ; also a great bush of another kind, covered with flowers, was 'immediately under the window, and kw Bell pointed to it at once. • - "Look, my lady! yon is th' rose he had in his ri coat. Bonny red and white, striped like a ri mackerel's back." They were parti-coloured roses, combining the York and Lancaster colours, and Silvia, who had never seen seen any like them before, had a great par- tiality for them. She looked at them thoughtfully for a minute or .4 two. "And what if I had ?—but I never did !" she f muttered, inconsequently. Then she drew her little figure up in proud and offended dignity— " You are a good girl, Bell, and you've done quite right to tell me, but you must never speak of , it to anyone else, never—now mind that—not to; - anyone ! Madam hates me,—that is no news. 814. she is welcome to do so. She cannot harm me. My husband will take care of that. I defy her— do you hear me, Bell, I defy her !" Bell was awed and astonished. No tragedy, queen could have hurled defiance at a foe with more innate force than did this tiny creature. "But she is no match for Madam, all the same," - mused the fisher lass on her homeward way, "it'll take th' two o' us to beat her, if it's to be managed • anyhow, 'A 'wm one with her wi' heart and soul. If it's to be a fight, that smooth spoken Madam 'll have to fight me and all !" (To be continued).

div.head: CHOOSING A VALENTINE.
div.p: CHOOSING A VALENTINE.
BY JEROME K. JEROME

Well, as I was going to say, talking about valen- - tines, a young may adore a young woman to dis- traction, but he does rot relish having to purchase and post to her a printed and published exposition of the fact. It requires a good doal of nerve to „. walk into a crowded shop and purchase a valentine. ' I used to have to do it myself once upon a time, and a most unenjoyable proceeding it was. I would , go in very red, and ask in a husky voice to see some. After looking over great traysful of what, in the langurtgB of the trade, are, I believe, termed " fourpenny," " sixpenty,” or "shilling sPntitnen- tale," and failing to find thereon any adequate ex- pression of my thoughts, I would blushingly observe • to the saleswoman that I rather fancied there was one in the window something like what I ivantedo and I would endeavour to describe its position. /„. But she never seemed able to understand me, and+ after taking down every one on the shelf but the , right one, she would be sure to say: "Perhaps you wouldn't mind just stepping into the street, and pointing it out, sir." Then I would creep out ci the door, feeling het all over; and, elbowing my way through the mob assembled about the window, would point the finger of desire towards the shameless, flaunting , thing. The crowd, intensely interested, would hustle round and read out the poetry aloud to each other, and the woman inside would smile and nedo and unhesitatingly take down and wrap up the wrong one; and 1, returning, would pay for it and put it in my pocket, and slink hurriedly awe'', hoping that St. Valentine's martyrdom had been an extra painful one. Once I thought I would get out of the difficultY by pretending it was for a child--a niece or a g9cl' daughter—that I wanted my valentine. A married friend of mine always used to send valentines W his children, and would walk into the shop and ask for them as bold as brass. "I want 'em very affectionate, if you pleasc;,"" would say to the young lady; "something with poetry." And he would pick out the most oat" rageously spooney ones that be could find-011 that I should have blushed to the roots of my br to be seen looking at—and coolly lay them with "Yes, that will do for Johnny ;' and "j'"' here's agood one for Nelly—young fellow. kneeling, and offering his heart and a velvet cushion to s girl ;" or, "This is the one baby will like—man shot I dead by a child with a bow and arrow. I'll take these three, my dear." (Ile used to call all girls "my dear." I know other married men who do tbe same. They go on anyhow, some of them.) —From" ihe Idler."

div.p: been guilty of persistent disobedience to the law, or corruption, Cr" maltersation; or opitression,-attinquiry should be held by judges; as in the case of an election petition, and should they 'find that the council had been guilty of tfie Xctitharged the members might be removed and their places be filled by persons appointed by the Lord Lieutetiant; In order to prevent reckless expendi- ture on office t,' road • Making, he proposed to establish a joint committee, ;whose assent should be obtained before any capital expenditure sanctioned by the county council should be made. The bill did not: deal with the police or, the urban sanitary, authorities. Mr. MettaXx, who followed,complimented Mr. Balfour on the clearness and limidity with which he had intro- duced the bill, but tiaid it was extraordinary that the Government, whose chief had just denounced the Lib- erals for wishing to give to the Irish majority power over the" more civilised" minority, should bring for- ward a measure for performing exactly the same opera- tion. The bill was less liberal and more reactionary than the one laid before the House by Mr. Lowther, and to give the judges power to try the County Councils was, he considered, a monstrous proposal. The Coercion Act created a new crime, but in this bill new crimes were to be created and brought home to elected bodies. The bill showed absolute distrust of the Irish ratepayers, and all he had to say was this, that he should like ill-Ailing better than that the Government should dissolve on it, and as soon as they liked. The measure was a monstrous impos- ture, a mockery, a falsification of pledges, and a just ground for new and fresh irritation in Ireland. Mr. J. Redmond held that the Bill was a sham and an insult ; and Mr. Justice WCarthy, said the measure was a pitiful farce, and likened the First Lord of the Treasury to a captain who had to fight the enemy and keep down the mutiny on board. The debate was then continued by Mr. MACARTNEY, Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, and Mr. T. HEALY. Sir Witti.tio HAR- COURT then rose and said the object of the Liberal party ought to be to Obtain the widest possible circulation of the measure, which was insulting. in its provisions. Mr. Balfour, in replying to the criticisms of the measure, said they showed that members opposise ha 4I made up their minds how they were going to receive the 13111 long before the proposals of thc Government were submitted. Mr. Chamberlain said he-preferred to see the Bill before pronouncing any opinion upon it. The Bill was read a first time, and the second reading set down for March 3.

COUNTY COUNCILLOR Dear Mester Rowlins, we shall want yo soon, To come an' grant eawr Earlestown chaps a boon; To lay eawr Public Hall's feaucdation stone, An' show the world heaw th' little teawu hes

grown; We met hey' axt Lord Stalbridge, but, yo see, lie's pitch a stickler fer ekonomy, That wen he twigg'd heaw bee the Rates wud goo., He'd very like ha' bagg'd a' Boss' or two I • Aw'll jot yo deawn wot programme we propose, Per makin' eawr Surveyor's bigger elm; An' pooin' him ereawt his present gloom, By findin' him MEI gradely elbow room. Fost, we've a mind to get eawr leadin' Sweep, (No deaubt, fer such a honor he'll cum cheap,) To tak his orgin, an' go car(o)lin' reaund, Invitin' theausands on to th' trystin' greaund. Then it will be yore turn to make a start, By gettin' th' secretary% do his part; Befoor the atone is "well an' truly laid," To read a list o' things fro ev'ry trade, That's goin' into that feaundation hole, Fro' Model Waggins to a Cob o' Coal. A soot o' clooas branded vri' a B, Per generations yet unborn to see; An' show um th' raison for a Public Hall, Is wen th' Surveyor's breeches get too small:! A vollum—Teknikal—spic, spon, an' new, On " Cookin' Neyt " an "Cookin' Figgers" too; To prove to aw thoose Nyowtou addle-pates, The greyt advantage o' increasin' th' rates:! A big Blue Bottle Fly, catch't wick an' seawnd, To keep on buzzin' ter a century reawnd.; An' born fur vverryin' the very guts Fro' pavin' stones or Bassilony nuts! A wizen't statue on th' Teetotal plan, To show heaw drinkin' pop can tuna man.; Make him a nuisance even friends men loathe, An' leave him crack't, an' stuntet in his growth. A plan meant for a railway sraitin' A danger an' a joke till th crack o' doom.;. In proof heaw some Directors earn ther fares, An give a doctor th' chance o' goeire shares! Then, wen yo'n getten ENV these things put in, , Yole think its time the gain' may wed l begin ; To set tun gooin', an' yore time tosave„ As leader, yo mun" rate] um off a stave.; " Praise up the Ileclifiss au' caw it nice, Make th' creawd believe it's very chep at th' price:; Puff Eater Commissioners ter raisin' Or sum, An' lettin' th' Nightsile go to kingdom come ! ' Gie urn ther due fer aw ther clever necks 0' duly scratchin' one another's backs; ' An' wen the Cheerrnon's on sum job bin' bent, Fur bein' oatber blind or wee! content. Aw darsay yole be gettin weary then, . . So yo can tor owd George to say " Amen !" Caw Carlin 'wi' his orgiu on the scene, To play up wile we sing— " GOD SAVE TELE QUEEN PliG 0. TUNS. Earlestowu, Feb. 19, 1892.

div.head: POLITICAL SPEECHES.
div.p: POLITICAL SPEECHES.

Sir William 'Harcourt, speaking on Wednesday night at a Liberal meeting in Whiteoltapet, said it would appear that the present session was to be devoted to another so-called remedial measure for Ireland, put which, he would venture to say. would be a sham and futile Local Government Bill. Referring to the recent division in the House. he ridiculed the canduct of busi- ness by Government leaders, and declared that to ,lay the fault upon the Whips was a mean and cowardly.de- vice. Having expressed his approval of the various items in the Newcastle prograinnte, Sir Wm. Harcourt said he looked forward with confidence to the time of dissolution, when an understanding people would pro- nounce the doom of the Unionist imposture and this reign of sham measures. MR. BALFOUR.

Mr. Balfour was the---ine-s-t-oir Wednesday night of the Constitutional Club, London, and, replyin., to the toast of his health, he asserted that the present Parliament had been one of almost unexampled utility. The reason why Gladstonians would not give anyeategorica.l utter- ances as to their Home Rule Bill was tkat they had not the slightest conception of what it was going to be. He believed they were waiting to see what the next general election might bring forth before they decided what it should be. If the Gladstonians gave theirish what they wanted they would be kicked from office by the English constituencies, If they did not give it, then they would be kicked from office by the Irish constituencies.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN, &C. –
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN, &C. -

Mr. Chamberlain, presiding on Wednesday afternoon at the third annual meeting of the Rural Labourers' League in London, said that in 1886 the friends of labour had a great disappointment, ,for then Mr. Gladstone suddenly sprang upon the country his Home Rule policy and from that moment the claims of labourers and all other reforms had been put aside in order to satisfy, the deMands of the Irish faction. When the majority of the I.iberal party followed Mr. Gladstone's lead they endea- voured to capture all the organisations of the party, and with incredible meanness e'deposed Mr. Jesse Collings from the chairmanship of the Allotments Association, which he had created. Being turned out of his seat by these political cuckoos. Mr. Collings proceeded to build another nest, and under his guidance the Rural Labour- ers' League had attained a position exceeding anythint, reached by the old Allotments Association. The Duke of DeYdnshire, in moving the adoption of the report, said that if permanent progress were to lae made in the work of bringing labourers into close tonn'ection with the soil it would not be by encouraging feelings of ill- ' will between classes, but it would be by a simultaneous endeavour,to improve the condition of every class in the community which was connected with the land. He looked to a reform in the transfer of land to produce an effect very much in the interests of the labouring classes. • LORD CROSS. Viscount Cross, addressing a Conservative meeting at West Derby on Wednesday night, :Is evidence of the prosperity of Ireland, . quoted the improved values of Irish railway stock. At present there were not in Ireland fifty boycotted farms, whereas five years ago nearly five theusand persons were suffering from boy- cotting. Ile claimed that for the artisans no party had done so much as the Conservatives, and he hoped that an Allotinenta Bill, whilst it might not prevent inigra.tiort of labourers to towns, would certainly benefit them. Peace and prosperity were the features of Lord Salis- bury's Admistration.
