div.head: EXAMINER, SATLIMAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATLIMAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1892.
I WARRINGTON LIBttA AMUClAlgotii

RECEPTION AND CONCERT. On Monday evening a reception and concert were held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-et., Warring- ton, under the auspices of the Warrington • Liberal Association. The reception wah held for the pur- pose of enabling Dr. Hoirston, Q.C., the Liberal can- didate for the borougb,and Mrs. Houston to become personally acquainted with all the officers and cap- tains, and their lady friends, of Latchford, Howley, St., Austins, and Whitecross Wards. There was a very numerous response to the invitations sent out. and between seven and eight o'clock, the time dur- ing which the reception lasted, there was a con- tinual Sow of visitors into the hall, Dr. and Mrs. Houston receiving and welcoming each one at the door. By eight o'clock„ the time at which the con- cert began,the hall was crowded: Mr. John Ryland s presided,and amongst others present besides Dr. and Mrs. Houston, were Mr. Theodore Fry, M.P. for Darlington; Miss Florence Daly, of Manchester; Mr. W. Pierpoint, Councillors J. H. Fleming, G. Blackhurst, H. Roberts. G. Plumotorti A. Browne; , Revs. IL Moore, J. W. Varley and J. Davies;. Dr. ' Gornall; Messrs. T. Morris, G. Severn, J. ,Winaer; , C. ' J. Holmes, T. Birchall, J. Walker, J. Longlauds, J.! , Gandy, J. 8.. Young, D. Tinnion, G. Legge, S. Jones,' W. Roberts, J. Titchett, S. &Stringer, F. Loughlin, ' F. R. Roberts, T. E. Kiernan, E. Ford, and•J. Clayton (Liberal agent). The CmtrasrAn, in opening the proceedings said he had received a telegram from Mr. F. A. Roberts ox- pressing his great regret at not being able to be present. He (the Chairman) had seen in the • Manchester Guar- dian" that morning a paragraph to theeffect that 16,000 more starving peasants had arrived in St. Petersburg, and that the Government had billeted them upon the householders and ordered them to supply them with food. (Laughter.) It did not say the Government were going to pay those householders,but he hoped they were. Nor did it say how many starving peasants had arrived before these, but it did seem an extraordinary thing to say that there were 16,000 more. Well, what did that mean.? It meant that there was something radically wrong in Russia' and he had no doubt it would explain a good deal of what they were told about the Nihilists and rebels of different kinds. (Bear, hear.) Probably if they were to ask the Tories, or many of them what they thought was the cause of that kind of thing they would say it must be bad Gcvern- ment—that Russia must be very badly governed and he would agree with them. Those things did not come about by accident. Then he thought of Ireland. Ire- land was not quite so bad as that, yet there was a time when Ireland was in a very bad way. But if they asked Tories what the cause of it was in Ireland they would likely say, "Oh, tbey are Irish people, and the fact is they are Roman Catholic; and then there are the agitators and the priests; you know you can d 3 no good with them." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He should not agree with the Tories then, because he would know that similar causes produced similar effects, and it was simply a question of the mode in which Ireland was governed. (Hear' hear.) They were told that Ireland was governed extremely well, that it was perfectly happy and contented, and in fact that Home Rule was dead. ft was implied that Home Rule was dead, but that we were ashamed to own it, but he thought they should teach the Tories a lesson. (Hear, hear.) They should let them see that Horne Rule was not dead, and that ,they were not ashamed that it was living. (Applause.) Be had been asked what he thought the prospects of the coming election were. Well, in former days they had had many ups and downs, probably more downs than ups, but Warrington changed a good dealin five years, and, as far as he could calculate,it changed for the better,or at least it had done so lately, and he did not see the slightest reason, pro- vided always they did their duty, why they should not return Dr. Houston at the next election. (Hear, hear and applause.' If they did, they should have a member of whom they could be proud. (Applause.) He sin- cerely 13oped that his attempted prophecy might come true. (Hear, hear and loud applause.) Mrs. Houston, and Miss Florence Daly, then sang " The Venetian song," in a style which at once won the admiration and approval of the audience. At the con- clusion of the song the applause was long and loud and was continued tillthe two ladies consented to repeat the ( song. Miss Valeria :Fleming also gave a pianoforte solo., in a way which evidenced great skill, and she was loudly applauded. Dr. HOUSTON, who was enthusiastically greeted, then addressed the meeting. Be expressed on hehalf of him- self and his wife the genuine pleasure which it had given them both to meet them all in the friendly manner in which they had met together that evening. (Hear, bear.) He thought they allowed a debt of gratitude to the gentlemen who conceived and to the gentlemen who so admirably carried out the arrangements for the meeting upon that occasion. It was, he understood, something of a new departure in the constituency,but he hoped that the opportunity afforded to the candidate and members of his family of meeting the more prominent of his. con- stituents on that occasion would not be lost, but that it would be repeated on future occasions. (Hear, hear.) He should just like to say a word or two about the present political situation. (Hear, hear.) Since he last had the pleasure of addressing an audience in Warrington, Parliament had assembled and they had an .opportunity of forming some • opinion of 1 what the Tory policy, or so-called policy, was. Of course it was the duty of a government to foreshadow more or less their policy in the speech from the throne and is duty bound as a loyal subject, he had read with SOMS care that speech from the throne. One subject was of course, treated in that speech with significent silence, namely, the subject which was agitating the minds of the electorate all over the three kingdoms—the legisla- tive independence of Ireland. (Hear. hear.) They gathered that the Tory and Unionist party were deter- miird to adhere with dogged tenacity to the explodea doctrine that the Union of Great Britain and Ireland WaS to beseeured not by the links which joined free people together—mutual respect, mutual affection, and unity of interests—but by the bonds that unite the master to the slave, the fetter and the lash, with an occasional largesse flung contemptuously to the recipient, wiling may indeed relieve temporary distress but winch left behind only humiliation and degradatioa. (Hear, hear.) That was the policy which the Tory party despite of all remonstrances, despite of all lessons, were :determined to adhere to, and that was the policy which they ill that meeting indignantly protested against. (Hear, hear and applause.) Coming to the subjects which were mentioned in the speech from the throne, the first thing thal struck one was that there was not one of the ineasures there foreshadowed that was the natural outcome of Tory policy, or the natural develop- ment of Tory principle. (Hear, hear.) There was not one of those measures which had net been denounced and decried by the leaders and the organs of the Tory party, and there was scarcely one of them which had not been discounted in advance by the Prime Minister himself. (Hear, hear.) Now, what could they espect from measures that were brought for ward under such circumstances? They were absolutely devoid of any inherent vitality, and they all knew that the Tory party took very good care that when they were introducing any measure of popu- lar reform, they introduced into it the seeds, if possible.

•of its its aeath,'and should any little spark of vitality sur- vive in it when it leaves the House of Commons then there was sonic Tory friend in the Upper House ready to give it its death-blow. (Hear, hear.) Just look at some of the measures that were foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. There was a reference to local govern- , I ment for Ireland, but how cautiously the subject was alluded to. They said that proposals would be brought before Patliament for extending to Ireland the principles of English local government. They knew very well what was the Tory ideas of the principle of local government. It was that the local landlord, with the assistance of the ' local parson, and with the support of the local brewer should have the whole matter in their own hands. (Hear, hoar and laughter.) A. question that was agitating the raral constituencies very much, the question of allot- ments for the agricultural labourers, that also was al- luded to, but they must remember that all that was to be taken with a grain of salt, because recently the Premier had been going about the country and saying, "Oh, you must have no compulsory purchase; the allot- ments must be the result of free contract," the meaning of which was that the beset landlord was to be able to boycott the measure out of existence. (Hear, hear.) Those were the measures which in the main were fore- shadowed by the Speech from the Throne, and what were they but shreds and notches of Liberal policy shamelessly stolen from Liberal politicians, joined clumsily, and then flaunted in the face of the country as, forsooth, a political programme? (Hear, hear' and applause.) Were the working-men, who now had the political power in their own hands, to be cajoled by tricks of that description? Be thought that the working-men had knowledge and perspicacity enough to see through plans and intrigues of that de- scription. (Hear, hear, and applause.) There was a time when people calling themselves Liberals would have been ashamed to ally themselves with a party who were pursuing a course of that kind. But times were changed. There was a time when such proceedings were de- nounced by Mr. Chamberlain in language as forcible as it was deserved, and yet they found that the Tory battle in the House of Commons was being fought by the Radical, Mr. Chamberlain. (Hear, hear, and hisses.) He did not think that it was a state of things that was likely to continue long. The questions had been asked in the House of Commons " Where was the Whig ? " and " Where was the Radical ?" He would ask" Where was the Tory ?" He thought the next general elediou would give a very good, a very complete, and a very satisfac- tory and a final answer to that question. (Hear, hear.) They were very near the general election, and it behoved them all to be ready for it. There might be a oye-election in that constituency, and he trusted that, if there was, they would all be ready for it But, whether it was to be a bye-election or the general election he did hope they would remember his words that an election might be sprung upon them. He had no doubt their opponents were on the qui eive ; that they were making their pre- parations and laying their plans possibly with a greater amount of knowledge than they (the Liberals) possessed, and it behoved them to be ready for any emergency. The workingmen had now a great opportunity, an opportunity which was, perhaps, not likely to be present again in this generation. They had the game in their own hands; they possessed the power which was so long withheld from them, and how they would use it was a matter which lay between them and their own consci- ences. But this he did say, that if by their votes at that election they perpetuated the system of coercion which existed in Ireland, and they perpetuated the system of oppression that really existed in the case of the working- classes, whether they were rural workingmen or whether they were the workingmen of the towns, upon them- selves the responsibility of that must rest. (Loud and prolonged applause.) The song "This work-a-day world " was then splen- didly sung by Miss Daly, and on being loudly recalled she gave, with fine expression," Come in and shut the door."

Mr. THEODORE Far, M.P., who was cordially wel- comed, next gave an address. He said that he felt it to be a great privilege and a great honour to be allowed to come over to Warrington to take some little part in the interesting proceedings of that gathering. He could assure them that they, in the neighbouring county of Durham, were looking forward with great interest to the elections that were about to take place in Lancashire. It was sometimes said that what Lancashire thought to- day England thought to-morrow, and there was a great deal in that. They looked forward with a very great deal of interest to the Rossendale elec- tion. (Applause.) He sat up till half-past twelve at night in order to hear the result, by telephone which was laid on to his house, and after he had got it he could assure them he went to bed and I slept the sleep of the just--(laughter)—and with a very great sense of gratitude to the good people of Rossendale for what they bad done for the cause of Home Rule in Ireland. (Applause.) At the last election there were four Unionist representatives sent to London from Lan- cashire, but at the present moment there was only one left. Sir Henry James was the solitary representative left, and he had been told that Sir Henry James would not be returned again for Bury. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt that they in Warrington had some hard work to do, but he did think that what Rossendale had done IVarrington could do, and if Rossendale could turn 1,400 on one side into nearly as many on the other side, the good people of Warrington could turn a majority of ' 500 on one side into more than a majority of 500 on the other side. (Hear, hear and applause.) England expected every man to do his duty to-day just as much as in the days of Nelson, and he believed that if they did their duty they would succeed in returning Dr. Houston to Parliament. (Applause.) He dare say that the election which was coming upon them was the most important election which they or he would ever see or pass through, because upon it would depend to a very large extent the giving to the Irish people that measure of justice which many of them believed the Irish people 'ought to have and one without which they will never be contented ; and he wanted them to remember that a gift given quickly and freely was twice as welcome as a gift which was wrung or extorted from an unwilling giver. ! (Hear, hear.) The Tories were very apt to tell them that they had given them this, that, or the other—the borough franchise, the Education Act, and other measures—but as lie uuderstoo 1 a free and willing gift there was no 1 giving whatever about it. It was not a gift in any sense I of the term. (Hear, hear.) Those measures were wrung out of the Tory party by the fear that if they did not give them some far larger measures of t he kind wouldbe passed. It was always the same with every measure of reform which the Tory party gave, and all of them were spoiled to a large extent by the clauses which they put in to prevent fully the from of these Acts, and they should never get trom the Tory party those measures which they •elieved.were requisite for the best interests of the people of tlys country. (Applause.) No mea- sure upon which the Liberal party had set its hand had ever been lost, for they had always carried to a success- ful issue those measures upon which they had set their mind. They were now culled upon to endeavour if possib!e to remedy the injustice which was done to the people of Ireland by the Act of Union. That Union was brought about by fraud and by bribery, and, so gross were the transactions of that day, that some succeeding- government bad destroyed all the correspondence and all the papers which were in existsnce in reference to that nefarious thing. (Hear, hear.) There was no repre- sentation of the Irish people at that time. Grattan's Parliament was simply elected by Protestants, the great bulk of the people being Roman Catholics, but having no voice whatever in the Government. Since

the Union they had had no fewer than 83 Coercion Bills which would not be tolerated in this country for a single moment. Home Rule had been thoroughly mis- represented in this country. It was simply the right of any nation to make laws for itself in things which en- tirely and exclusively belonged to itself. The Irish did not want to have anything to do with the army and navy, or colonial or foreign policy, with the laving of duties and tariffs, coining, and a great variety of other subjects of an imperial character. Ireland wanted only this one simple thing—to be allowed to discuss those subjects which entirely belonged to Ireland. (Hear,hear.) If they wanted to see how Ireland had been misgoverned they could see it in a great variety of ways, in the num- ber of families which had been evicted from their homes, and in the diminution of the land un- der culture, all of which tended to show that Ireland had been badly governed in the past. (Hear, hear.) In this great empire there were already something like 31 Parliaments, and was it likely that the establishment of one more, which, after all, was little more that the London County Council, was going to disintegrate the Empire. The great British Em- pire was not going to be disintegrated quite so soon as some of those people imagined. That was only a kind of Aunt Sally that was put up to be knocked down again. (Laughter and applause.) Since 1841 no fewer than 3,888,000 people had been evicted from their homes in Ireland, 1,250,000 had died of famine in that country, and more than 4,000,000 had emigrated to other parts of the world, and it was estimated by the eminent stat- istician, Mr. Mulhall, that these Irish emigrants would have made wealth in other places amounting to more than £685,000,000. (Hear, hear.) Was it not likely that these people had been driven from Ireland by the result of English misgovernment and misrule. (Hear, hear.) He believed that, when the time ca.me,the democracy of this country, the people of Warrington ' included, would cast their votes on the side of justice and on the side of freedom. (Loud applause.) Having re- feriod to the question of the agricultural labourer, Mr. Fry concluded by sayitg that they could have no man as a candidate who more thoroughly understood these questions than Dr. Houston, and if the people of War- rington reversed their representation they would never regret it. (Loud applause.) Mr. W. H. Wallington then sang in a capital manner "Ho! Jolly Senkin," and Mr. W. Ford gave a reci- tation in the Lancashire dialect which caused great amusement, and for which he was very loudly ap- plauded. Mrs. Houston next sang Gounod's "Entreat me not to leave thee" in a way which at once proved her to be a vocalist of a very high order. The feelings of the audience were evidenced by their enthusiastic acclamations, and in response to the very docided recall Mrs. Houston gave "The wearing of the green" with an appropriateness of expression which captivated her hearers. It should here be added that the accompani- ments on the piano were all played in an excellent man- ner loy Mr. W. FL Payton. Mr. W. PIERPOINT proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers, and singers, and accompanist. and Councillor A. Baowiaa seconded this proposal which was carried with acclamation. Mr. Fry having responded, there were cries for Mrs. Houston to acknowledge the vote on behalf of the ladies, but that lady appeared to be disinclined to undertake the rote of a public speaker, and consequently Dr. Houston responded in her stead, and also proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman. This was seconded by Councillor H. Roberts, and warmly accorded. The response of the Chairman brought this very pleasant and highly successful gathering to a closo.
RECOLLECTIONS t )F SPURGEON

BY AN OLD NEWTONIAN. On Easter Sunday morning, 1861, I went with a friend to hear Mr. Spurgeon preach his first sermon in the new Tabernacle, London. There were several reasons that impelled me to go and hear him. First: I was anxious to see the building of which Rumour had spoken so loudly and favourably as to its mag- nificent accoustic qualities; and for once I found Rumour had spoken nothing but truth. It was a sublime treat to hear about six thousand voices singing without organ or other instrument some of the grand old Psalm tunes of which Mr. Spurgeon was so fond. To hear it once was to never for- get it. tlecondly: I had heard frequently that the , preacher resorted to all sorts of buffooning to im- press his audience with his meaning; such for in- stance as " sliding" down the bannister of the stairs leading on to his preaching platform (he had no pulpit) to illustrate "going to hell "; and crawl- ing up the stairs to illustrate "going to heaven." I confess I saw nothing of the sort. The only start- ling thing that occurred was his way of dealing with a sleeper. I remember isis words well. He was in the middle of a fiery passage, when he sud- denly stopped, and pointing to somewhere in the body of the church, he remarked: "I see a sleeper before me! It may be that on this particular occa- sion there are many strangers present, who are unaware of my habit with regard to sleepers; and for that reason I refrain at this time from taking my usual course; but I now give notice that from hencefortn, should I observe any one sleeping dur- ing my ministration on this platform, I shall make him "the observed of all observers." That Mr. Spurgeon had a weakness for playing on words, I think no one will deny. I remember on one occasion he was discoursing on the subject of "Good fathers having bad sons ;" and after men- tioning David and Absolom, and some others, which Ido not at the moment recollect, he said that " Even Noah had a Ham in the Ark !" Of course there was a titter up and down the Church, which lather grated on my ears; but the joke was soon forgotten when he was once more in the full swing of a magnificent oration. I have heard many preachers in my time, but none to equal Spurgeon ; and I recall one sermon in particular, where he was replying to some attacks made upon him by a couple of ted-hot Ritualists. I wished many a time they had been where 1 was. I fancy that they would in future have been less glib in their abuse of a far greater man than them- selves. His calling upon the shades of Luther, ' Wycliffe, and Melancthon to purge the Church of England of its idolatrous sacerdotalism, and to turn it " from the path that leads to Rome" is ringing in my ears even as I write. It was almost equal to an electric shock. No wonder that the Tabernacle was crowded when he was the m;nister ; and those who were privileged to hear him, could not but be immensely impressed with his tremendous power land his overwhelming earnestness. His very large share of egotism could readily be forgiven, for he was after all but human, as he would have been the first to confess. I fear we may say of him that " We shall never see his like again:, February 15, 1892.

The death is announced at Etnsworth, on Saturday, of Admiral of the Fleet Sir Provo Wallis, at the age of 101. Sir Provo was born in 1791, and entered the navy in 1804. In 1851 he became Rear-Admiral ,Vice-Admiral in 1857, Admiral in 1863, and Admiral of the Fleet in 1875. He served Gn board the Cleopatra. in 1810 at the capture of Guadaloupe, for which he received a medal, and was lieutenant of the Shannon when she captured the American frigate Chesapeake in 1813. Afterwards he commanded the vessel, the captain having been seriously wounded and the senior lieutenant killed. For this he was promoted and specially thanked by the Ad- miralty. From 1847-51 he was aide-de-camp to the Queen. In 1860 he was created K.C.8., and G.C.B. in 1873. Sir Provo Wallis married in 1817 Julia, daughter of the late Yen. Archdeacon Massey, who died in 1848. Re afterwards married in 1849 Jemima, daughter of the late General Sir R. T. Wilson, M.l'.
1.0.U.T.-NO. I CONVENTION, SOUTH
WEST LANCASHIRE,

The annual session was held in the Lecture Hall, Cross-lane, Earlestown, on Saturday. In the absence of the C.C.T. (Bro. Colour-Sergt. T. Mantle, Wardiigton), the C.C., Bro. Quartermaster-Sergeant J. W. Roberts, of Warrington, presided. The Cre- dential Committee reported 68 representatives pre- sent from various parts of the district, including Warrington, St. llelens, Earlestown, Hindley, Peas- I ley Cross, Fir's-lane, and Widnes. The following resolution was passed by silent vote :—" That this convention, representing 760 Good Templars (adult and juvenile) in the 16 Lodges of South West Lancashire district, at its annual ses- sion assembled, respectfully tenders to our beloved Queen and to their Royal Highnesses I the Prince and Princess of Wales our loyal sympathy and heartfelt condolence in the great sorrow inflicted by the early death of his Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence and Avondale." Simllar resolutions were passed, and copies, signed by the C.C.T. and Secretary, ordered to be for- warded to the relatives of the late Cardinal Manning and the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon. The Con. Sec. (Bro. R. Kean, Warrington) reported an increase of three lodges and 95 members. The treasurer (Bro. Brock- bank, St. Helens) reported the funds in a better condition than they were 12 months ago. The election of officers resulted in a majority of the retiring officers being re-elected. In the evening th-t usual tea and public meetings were held, the Rev. T. W pine-Jones, of Earlestown, presiding, and excellent speeches were delivered by the Chairman and Mr. Dring, ef Earlestown, interpersed with songs, readings, and recitations, the following taking part : Sisters Whity, laden, and Willis ; Brothers Edwards, Kean, Clarke Skaife, and jtosy Sheath.

div.head: MR. GLA.DSTONE'S RETURN.
div.p: MR. GLA.DSTONE'S RETURN.

In view of the severe weather, and the possibility of ts return, it is felt undesirable that Mr. Gladstone should come back to town in accordance with his avowed intention. Letters were despatched to him on Tuesday begging him to extend his stay in the south for a week or two longer, his colleagues on the Front Bench being able to assure him that there is in the political situation no immediate necessity for his return.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AND OLD AGE PENSIONS.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AND OLD AGE PENSIONS.

Mr. Gladstone, having received from a correspondent a scheme in regard to old age pensions, writes—" Dear sir, I have received your letter, and I thank you for your kind words. lam glad that the condition of the aged working classes is receiving the attention which is due to it, but I am sure you will agree that on a subject so vast in extent and consequences much consideration is needed in order to arrive at safe concLisions.—Your very faithfully, W. E. GLADSTONE."

div.head: ST. HELENS MINERS AND THE COAL
div.p: ST. HELENS MINERS AND THE COAL
CRISIS.

Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, St. Helens, has received from the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation the forms of notice to all the colliery pro- prietors in his district for the cessation of work. The notices, which will be posted on Sunday night, so as to be received by the employers on Monday morning, point out the decision of the National Conference, and continues, "We thersfore give you 14 days' notice to cease all contracts; the notice to expire on the 12th March, 1892 ; we remain, yours, the Colliers, and all underground workpeople in your employ." The notices will affect over 2,000 miners in the St. Helens district.

div.head: DEATH OF THREE II.P.'S.
div.p: DEATH OF THREE II.P.'S.

Mr. F. A. flankey, M.P., for the Chertsey Division of Surrey, died on Monday morning after a few days' illness. Mr. Hankey, who was a Conservative, was born in 1833.—The Press Association's correspondent t/elegraphs that Mr. Wardle, M.P., died on Tuesday morn- ing. Mr. Wardle, who was a Liberal, had sat for South Derbyshire since 1835. Mr. Wardle had been ill for some time, from the after effects of influenza ; but the immediate cause of death was gout and kidney disease. He recently announced that he would not seek re-elec- tion, and the candidates for the vacant seat are Mr. Evans, Broad Liberal, and Mr. Be.resford Melville, Con- servative.

iinaes " second edition telegram states that Sir George Campbell, M.P., died on Wednesday, at Cairo. Sir George was a Liberal, and had sat for Kirkcaldy since 1875. The deceased, who was born in 1824, was for some time Lieut.-Governor of Bengal. He had sat for Kirkcaldy district since April, 1875, as a Liberal. His majority over the Liberal Unionist is 1886 was 1,103, and in 1885 he polled 2,180 votes, as compared with 1,504 given to another Liberal candidate, and 746 given to the Conservative.

div.head: LADY CHARGED WM( MURDER.
div.p: A LADY CHARGED WM( MURDER.

At Coleraine, on Tuesday evening, Coroner Caldwell committed for trial at Londonderry Assizes, Mrs. Anna Margaret Montagti, wife of Mr. Atcheson Montagu, of Cramore House, Coleraine, on a charge of causing the death of her daughter, Mary Helen Montagu. aged three years. At the inquest evidence was given to the effect that on Saturday the child's gorerness locked her in a dark room as a ponishment for some childish offence. Mrs. Montagu came in later, and tied the child's arms behind her back with a stocking, to which she. affixed a string, and fastened it to a ring in the wall. Three hours later Mrs. Montagu went to the door of the room and called the child by name, but receiving no response went in and found the child loaning, forwards. She unfastened her and carried her to a bedroom and endeav- oured to restore animation, but life was then extinct. The medical evidence was that death was caused by strangulation. Mr. Montagu reported the matter to the constabulary, and several constables were sent to the house and remained there until the inquest. Mrs. Montagu, who is daughter-in-law of Lord Robert Montagu, was allowed bail.

div.head: HORRIBLE BRUTALITY TO A GIRL
div.p: HORRIBLE BRUTALITY TO A GIRL

The county magistrates at Helston (Cornnwall) were on Wednesday occupied for some hours in hearing a ease , which has excited intense interest and indignation in the locality. Mrs. Elizabeth Rowe was charged with cruelty i to her stepdaughter, a girl of thirteen, who lived with her at a mill which Mrs. Howe had inherited. For a long time there had been rumours that the girl was cruelly treated, and some distant relatives having at length in- tervened, found that the child had been subjected to great btutality and was in a very emaciated condition. Among other cruel treatment she had been frequently strapped up to a beam and thrashed continuously with • a thick whip. On one occasion she was stripped late at night and one hand was tied above her head and the other behind her back, and she was left here despite her pleadings throughout the night. When released she was brutally flogged. The girl had been forced by her step- mother to eat a candle and swallow brine aMi soapy water, and pepper had been throw-it in her eyes. She had also been made it for a long time in cold the weatherpro. up to her neck in water. The intent allegpd,by h secution was to endanger her health and thus benefit the accused pecuniarly. To the atoniehtnent of those in court a fine of £lO only was inflicted.

Judging from Mr. BALFOUR'S speech on Thursday night,there is every reason tobelieve that they are • about to repeat their blunder in dealing with the Iquestion of local self-government. They are offer- ing the Irish a stone when they ask for bread; and profess to be lost in wonder that they aro not ' satisfied. Lord SALISBURY has compared them to ' Hottentots; and the other day he described the : great bulk of them as uncivilised. Yet after all

- - this, he expects them to fall in with his views as to the m magement of their affairs! Coercion, per- Petual coercion, is the only course which the Prime Blinizter can consistently take, having regard to the Opinions he has expressed ; and it is because this is so that we distrust the new Local (3vernment Bill for Ireland. We cannot bring ourselves to believe that the Tories intend to Pass any measure which will give more power to the people of Ireland. No, the Bill is to be used as so much dust to be thrown into the eyes of the English electors. They want to go before the country saying—" See what we were about to do for Ireland, if the chance had been given us." The answer to that is—" You have had your chance ; You have been office six years; but you have broken your pledges and betrayed your trust. Ilegone ! for you have done the things which you Ought not to have done, and left undone th 3 things You ought to have done, and their is no health in You."

1 , APpointmentof _ , THE House of Commons was occu- pied, on Tuesday, with the discus- magistrates. sion of a most important reform ; ibut the Tories would have none of it because it ; happened to be of a thoroughly democratic kind. Mr. SEALE lIAYNE moved the second reading of ' the bill which had for its object an improvement iU the appointment of Justices of the Peace. The main feature of the bill WAS that which sought to give power to County Councils and Town Coun- cils to elect a certain number of magistrates in Proportion to the number of inhabitants. It also Provided for the Chairmen of Boards of Guar- -4ians and Rural Sanitary' Authorities becoming justices during the period of their office—on the aalne principle as that on which Mayors and Alder- men of certain towns become justices. It was sought besides to abolish the property qualifica- tion which at present attaches to the office of county magistrates. The absurdity of retaining a Property qualification is manifest when it is re- inernbered that no such qualification is required in , the case of the election of a member of Perlis- ' ruent. Property is the fetish of Toryism, and ought to be knocked on the head whenever it in- terferes with the exercise of the rights of citizen- !hip. Who is there who has not observed, and peen ashamed to observe, that some hare-brained stripling, who has not yet sown his wild oats, has been made a magistrate simply because of family influence ? With an eye to such inequality and injustice, Burns might well exclaim— Ye see yon birkie, ca'd a lord Wha struts, and stares, and a' that; Though hundreds worship at his word, He's but a coof for a' that. At present it is left to Lord Lieutenants to appoint county magistrates, and to the Lord Chancellor to appoint magistrates for boroughs, While it is notorious that the chief consideration is party service rather than fitness for the office. Indeed it is no uncommon thing for local politi- cians to begin to advance what they call their claims to the honour, after subscribing and work- ittg f'4r one party or the other for a number of I,aars- If report speaks truly, it has.been one of the ,burdens of Sir Gilbert Greenall's life to be Pestered with applications for his influence, by men Who have been great on their "claims." What honour, forsooth, can there be in an appointment Under such circumstances? And what sort of Magistrates are they likely to make who are so lacking in self-respect ? It is a 'natter of course to say that the bulk of the magistrates throughout the country are , Tories ; and this is the case, too, in Wales where Liberalism so largely prevails. However qualified by means, ability, and character a man may be in the Principality he is under a boycott for the c°unty bench, if he happens to be a Dissenter. l'en the Home Secretary was constrained to admit, in the course of the debate, that he had tied to put pressure upon Lord Lieutenants in ales with a view to the appointment of qualified ...Nonconformists. What a revelation is that con- lession of the viciousness of the present system I It certainly ought either to be abolished or sup- rernented as proposed by the Bill which was be- Ore Parliament on Tuesday. But the Tories never do anything in the way of reform except 1-11:10ti compulsion,or through fear ; so the word was Passed that the bill must be thrown out, and 111 thrown out it was by a majority of 43, Mr. CHAIM ; 41?ItLAIN and his dwindling followers voting with he Governm eat. So be it; it is an object lesson '' for the democracy.

And why should it not be so ? As the schoolteacher is not paid to give any but secular instructions, it is an imposi- tion upon him to burden him , with:any other compulsory duty. Let the cobbler stick to his last. We fully recognise that Catholics , will be at a disadvantage unless some such:plan be adopted as that in operation in Minnesota, for, if they do not come under School Boards, they will have to carry on their own schools whilst contributing as tax- payers to the support of the School Board System. It would be interesting to know what our Catholic friends think of the arrangement sanctioned by Archbishop Ireland. It seems to us, so far as we can judge of it, to bridge the chasm in a satisfac- tory way.

The pinch of poverty is being felt at St. Helens, owing to the stoppage of the Union Plate Glass Works, and the reduction in the number of men employed at the Chemical Works. It is hoped that some of the men will be called in to assist in the construction of the St. Helens and South Lan- cashire Railway ; but whilst the grass grows the horse starves. The outlook is therefore a gloomy one.

Nothing now-a-days is sacred. Two men were brought before the magistrates, on Monday, at Chester, for fighting, in St. John's churchyard, on the previous Saturday night. There was a time when such men would have fought rather than be taken to the place of graves in the night- -the witching hour of night When churchyard/I' yawn esnd hell itself breathes out Contagion to this world. The fear of all that seems to have gone ; but it is no sign of improvement to use God's acre as a prize ring.

The influerza has a deal to answer for. It caused Peter Robinson of Warrington to try to keep his spirits up by pouring spirits down. Ho seems to have taken an over-dose of his medicine, for under its influence he was led to take the Nuis- ance Inspector by the coat, whilst he proceeded to abuse him. However, the magistrates were in a merciful mood; they simply bound Robinson over, evidently thinking that a man who suffered from the blight was sufficiently punished.

The revocation, on Tuesday, of the muzzling order is a great relief to dogs and their owners. ,‘ Love me, love my dog" still holds good, for there are some men who would almost as soon be muzzled themselves as have their pet muzzled. However, if the restriction has resulted in reduc- ing the loss of life from hydrophobia the public will have reason to be thankfvl, for, after all, one human being is of more value than many dogs.

There were two muncipal bye-elections in Liver- pool on Tuesday. In Rodney Ward, Mr. William- son, the Liberal candidate, was returned with a majority of 359, a majority more than three times that of the last election in the Ward. In Everton Ward, the Tories were fighting amongst themseves. In their speechifying after the poll, they got to calling each other traitors. It may be they are right in using such language; they ought to know each other.

If landlords could only be frightened into put- ting the dwellings they own in a sanitary condi- tion,then would the world grow healthy. They are certainly liable at law for negligence. On Satur- day, the Queen's Bench and a special jury a warded a man and his wife £77 10s. It was shown that they had lost their four children, and been made ill themselves through the house they lived in be- ing in an insanitary condition. It would seem that the Bench hadn't power to hang the landlord : but they did what they could in the way of punish- ing him.

Mr. Robert Pierpoint, the Conservative candi- date for Warrington, is far from being in fighting trim although he has a hard fight before him. With a view to improving his health, he has been advised to go to Malta, and is now on his way to that salubrious island of the Mediterranean. He doesn't expect an immediate dissolution, or he would try a recruiting ground nearer Warrington. It doesn't look either as if that "pleasant sur- prise "in the shape of a peerage for Sir Gilbert Greenall is going to "come off." Can it be that those who have to determine these matters have come to the conclusion that the peerage has had enough of " beerage F"

Now that the Warrington Water Works are the , of the Corporation, the question is raised -,Lier it would not be advisable to lower the ate to manufacturers who may be called large consumers, although they may not reach the enormous consumption of 28,000,000 gallons, the minimum, at present, for obtaining the benefit of a reduced rate from 9d. to 6d. per 1,000 gallons. Why should there not be a sliding scale from 9d. to 6d. based upon the quantity consumed? At present the manufacturer who uses 20 million gal- lons per year is charged at the same rate as the man who uses 20 thousand gallons.

1 The matter has been brought home to Messrs. W, A. Bishop and Co., who have commenced loperations at the Dial-st. Mill, Warrington, as I borax manufacturers. Here is the case as it pre- sents itself to them. They say The first obstacle encountered is that of the water supply. We have a well with good water, but if the Corporation will supply us at 64. instead of 9d. a thousand gallons we will not use it. The amount i we shall pay s £35 per annum,and we shall consume 20 or 30 thousand gallons per week. The rule hither- to acted upon is that manufacturers in Warrington, in order to obtain water at 6d. (which is what Liver- pool is paying, whilst Glasgow only pays 5d.) must I use £7OO of water per annum, or 28,000,000 gallons, I a sheet of water :one mile long, 200 ft. wide, and 6ft. 1 deep; or, taking the consumption at 12 gallons a head per day, equal to the consumption of 5,600 of inhabitants, that is one-tenth of the population of Warrington. Can it be true that this policy is keep- ing manufacturers away instead of attracting them to the town of Warrington And with water run- ning to waste, have the members of the Water Committee a right to refuse an income of £35 per annum, which might go towards the reduction of the rates? £7OO per annum, the limit imposed, means the interest at 3i per cent, on a capital of £20,000. This is a large order to ask individuals coming to Warrington to comply with.

--- - A miner named Michael Walsh, was fined 10s. and costs, at Newton, on Saturday, for smoking in the Edge Green mine belonging to Messrs. Evans and Co. Considering that the mine is a fiery one, and has previously been the scene of an explosion, it is not too much to say that the fine was altogether inadequate. If the man had been risking his own life only, the offence would have been of comparatively small moment; but there were 200 miners in the pit when this foolhardy fellow risked a catastrophe by liglating his pipe. He deserved to be flogged or sent to gaol for a month. Leniency in such cases may be the pre- lude to disaster.

Preaching in Liverpool, on Sunday, at the Church for the Blind, the Rev. T. W. M. Lund let it be knownthat, in his view, sentimental feelings as to animals should not stand in the way of bene- fits to human beings. Referring to the anti- vivisection crusade, he said "It seemed that the country preferred the death of our best men to a

It may be said of the Liberal reception at the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, on Monday even- ing, as " Artemus Ward" said of Shakespeare's grave, namely, that it was a success. Dr. and Mrs. Houston seemed " to the manner born" in receiving visitors; everybody was in good hu- mour ; the room was crowded, and the proceedings were most enthusiastic. Rumour had been busy with the name of Mrs. Houston as a vocalist ; but she acquitted herself in manner which was beyond all expectation. It was a treat, too, to listen to Miss Florence Daly, of Manchester, while Miss Valeria Fleming was not less successful on the piano. Indeed, every item on the pro- gramme—speeches included—merits the wor(" " admirable." As there is to be another reception on Monday night next, it is a matter of course to say that there will be another crowded gathering. --- Mr. Balfour was profusely apologetic, on Thurs- day night, in introducing the Irish Local Govern- • aent Bill; and he had need to be, for a more wretched measure of the first order was never laid before Parliament. It is as full of make-shifts and devices as Mr. Disraeli's "fancy-franchise " bill ; and is evidently designed to prevent the people of Ireland acting as free citizens. It is "a monstrous imposture," as Mr. Morley termed it— "a thing of shreds and patches." Sir William Harcourt said it might be intended as a huge joke, but he thought it was carrying the joke too far. The Government promised similarity to the Eng- lish Bill; but it is no more like the English Bill than cheese is like chalk. It has been conceived in the "Hottentot" vein of the Prime Minister, and,as it is an insult to the Irish nation, it may be of service in uniting the Nationalists and the Parnellites in re-modelling it, or, if it cannot be re-modelled, in fighting it to the bitter end.

HALTON-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The annual congregational tea party was held in the schoolroom, Mill Brew, on Monday evening, and there was such a large number for tea that there had to be a "second sitting." The Rev. W. Arrowsmith presided over the after proceedings. He said he had found warm and loving friends in Runcorn, and as loyal a body of officials as he had met anywhere. He was gratified at the excellent evening attendance at chapel, and he urgc them to improve the morning attendance. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Hanby, Messrs. S. Pope and J. R. Frith.—Mr. J. Ince read the financial statement which showed contributions £lO in advance of last year. A capital programme of music was gone through. UMBRELLAS EECOYERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Saukey-st., Warrington.—Advt. INTERESTING PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN. On Wedn, day evening last, the teachers and senior scholars in connection with the Free Methodist Sunday School met together in the schoolroom, Ellesmere-at. Mr. F. Clarke, the assistant superintendent, presided, and expressed his pleasure at seeing such a large gather- ing, and called upon Mr. J. Eolford, who said it was 19 years since he was appointed assistant secretary, and for 18 years he had held the post of secretary,so that he had been pretty closely associated with the management of the school for a long period. There were those present who could look back with him to the varying experi- ence through which they had passed, and lie was sure that they would all feel grateful to God for the pros- perity that had attended their labours in connection with the school. The mind, he said, had a powerful habit of associating men and movements. If the abolition of slavery was the tonic,we naturally thought of Wilberforce and so on. No reference to the history of Free Metlio- , dism in Runcorn, and especially, as they were now con- sidering it in relation to Sunday school work, would be complete without reference to their highly-esteemed friend, Mr. Gandy, who had served the school in the capacity of superintendent for 17 years, having for the five years previous been assistant superintendent. They all admired the splendid qualities of heart and mind which Mr. Gandy possessed, and he (Mr. Holford) felt it an honour to be entrusted by them that, evening with the duty of asking Mr. Gandy to accept,as a small token of their esteem, the marble clock and pair of bronze ornaments which he then uncovered and which bore the following inscription :—" Presented to Mr. E. Gandy by the teachers and scholars of Ellesmere-st. Sunday school as a small token of their appreciation of his life-long devotion to the welfare of the school. Runcorn, Febru- ary 17th, 1892." Mr. Gandy, in acknowledging the pre- sentation,said he could not find words adequately to ex- press his feelings ; he was deeply grateful for this mark of their esteem, but he was quite taken by surprise as he never expected any reward until he got to heaven. He thanked those present from the bottom of his heart, and said that this memento would be an encouragement to him to labour on for the welfare of the school, as it was a very dear spot to him,and he hoped to spend many , happy years in their midst. The Rev. J. Martin and Mr. I. Stubbs also addressed the meeting. A selection of vocal and instrumental music was contributed by Mrs. Newall, Misses Marlow ,Newall, and K. Paul, and Messrs. ' J. Holford and T. Parry. Miss Paul officiated as accom- panist. Mr. I. Stubbs gave a reading in the Lancashire , dialect, after which the company sat down to a splendid tea which had been provided by the ladies.
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD AND ITS WATER CHARGES.

Yesterday, His Ho-r—o—u-r--ge Shand, gave hi judgment at Widnes County Court in the case brought by the Widnes Local Board, against several builders and others with regard to the minimum charge for water supplied by meter. He gave a verdict for the Local Board on all points, with costs. Mr. Oppenheim applied for costs on the higher scale, but His Honout declined to accede to the request.

PROMOTION OF SHPT, LARGE. In consequence of the retirement of Sept. Plant, of Middlewich, a vacancy has occurred, and the Chief Constable has selected Supt. Large, of Run- corn, to fit it. Iliddlevvich is a very extensive and important division, being the second largest divi- sion in the county, and Sunt. Large fully deserves I the promotion and the honour. lie came to Runcorn ' three years ago, when the police and the public were most antagonistic but by Mr. Large's tact, urbanity,and straightforward conduct a better state of affairs soon prevailed, and he leaves the town with the good wishes of the townspeople,who,while gratified at his promotion, are sorry to los,. him. His successor will be Inspector Atherton,of Dukin- field, an officer who spent some months in the town about six years ago, and who is well and favourably known. THE PROFITS OF BICYCLII DEA LERS.

It trans- pired during the hearing that the plaintiff's profits on the bicycles in each of the cases were nearly 100 per cent.—His Honour gave judgment for the plain- tiffs in the first case for .£2, in the second for £l, and in the third for _E2 10s. with costs. PRESENTATION TO MR. JAMES LITTLER AT :RUNCORN. The choristers of Runcorn Parish Church have pre- sented Mr. James Littler,their respected conductor, with a silver mounted baton in acknowledgement of his efficient services.

NEWTON. " At a meeting of the Finance and General Purposes Committee of the Newton Division Conservative Association held at the offices, Newton, on Saturday, the appointment of registration agent in place of Mr. W. Holbrook, who has resigned, was dealt with. The 11 applications had been reduced to tl ree, viz., Mr. Wilding (Liverpool), Mr. Hyde (St. Helens), and Mr. W. Mawdsley (Earlestown). These gentlemen were individually called before the committee, and in the result, Mr. Mawdsley was appointed. Mr. Mawdsley has for some years been an energetic worker in the Conservative cause, and he has re- ceived congratulations upon his appointment from all sides.

Newtotli Warburton, and let out a valuable calf. It was sden by one of his men after 11 o'clock, and he gave it chase in the hope of penning it again. The calf ran the wrong way, making straight for lleatley Station and dashing into the turngate just as the midnight mail passed, smashed one of the bars, which proved to be rotten, and got on the line. The signalcc an at once "closed the line" and telegraphed to Dunham, where it was also closed, and then began a chase. assisted by a couple of railway porters. The frolic- some calf kept the men on the run for a couple of hours, and datained a couple of trains for nearly the same time, until its capture was effected near Dunham Station. SHOCKING FATALITY AT WIGAN.

On Thursday a shocking fatality took place at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles's Moss Arley Pit,Lower Ince, Wigan, a wagon-lowerer named Joseph Pen- nington being found entangled in the cog wheels of a slack elevator. His body was dreadfully mangled. How he got into the wheels is unknown. EvAN's GREAT STOCKTAKING SALE now on,-17 S .rkey- -8 t., Warrlngton.—Adat. NEW MAGISTRATES. On Wednesday, at the Preston Sessions, Mr. Thos. Liberals about to move, or who have moved from one room or house to another since the 15th of July last, should at once send notice to the agent or secretary of the local Liberal orginization. If the removal be from one borough to another, the Liberal organisation in each borough should receive notice. Elections are often lost solely through neglect to notify changes of address. CHESHIRE *COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. MEETING OF RUNCORN LIBERALS.
MR. SPEAKMAN REPLIES TO HIS ACCUSER.

The adjourned meeting of the Liberals of Run- corn was held in the Union Hall, Regent-st., on Saturday night. There was a good attendance, and Mr. J. R. Frith again occupied the chair. Amongst those present were Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., W. Ockleston, W. Stanmay, B. Kniveton, E. W. Hum- phreys, A. Norman, W. Carroll, T. Poole, T. Clegg,T. Lea, J. Lea, W. Betney, 11. Wright, W. Ilandley,and John Clark and A. Riley (division secretaries). A discussion took place as to whether the meeting was a public one of Liberals or only of members of the council, and the chairman ruled that the meeting was public.—Mr. Kniveton moved that the meeting be not reported.—Mr. Poole seconded.—Mr. W. Carroll moved 1 and Mr. Billington seconded an amendment that the proceedings be reported, and this was carried. MR. SPEAKMAN'S DEFENCE.

Mr. Speakman, who was receivsd in applause, said circumstances over which he had ao control prevented him from being present on Wednesday evening. It seemed to him that he was on his defence for his conduct in the County Council during the past three years. He denied the charge that he was not a sound Liberal, but was sitting on the hedge feeling ready to go over one way or the other. His Liberalism might not be Mr. Knive- ton's standard, but he had always been known as a Liberal, aid he hal

ALWAYS VOTED LIBERAL. (Applause.) During the three years there had been ten divisions on the Council, and out of this number there was only one that could be said to be coloured by any political feeling, and he con- sidered that he had no case to answer, in the way Mr. Kniveton had put it. He did say there was a little chaff about the vote spoken of, but one of the members, the treasurer of Northwich Division Liberal Association, at once put the meeting right by telling them that he had always supported the Liberal cause not only with his presence bUt with his purse. (Applause.) Seeing that they had no politics in the Council, he failed to see why this onslaught should have been made upon him, and how a Mr. Millington could say, unless he wanted to

AIR HIS ELOQUENCE, that his Liberalism stood discredited. Mr. Handley had said that he (Mr. Speakman) admitted having made a mistake in his voting. He could not admit this in the least. The question of

THE CONTROL OF THE POLICE was under discussion, and he argued that, as the council was only three months old, it was not time to begin to interfere with the Act of Parliament which the council could only administer, but as time went on they would know the business better, and could tackle the case with greater intelligence. He did vote against this, and gave his reason at the time. As time progressed the subject ripened, and he was happy to toll them that he was one of the committee to settle the question of the court of appeal, and now if any policemen had griev- ances they could, and did, appeal to get justice. At the last election two Liberals fought the constituency he now represented. Those acwainted with the circum- stances knew that it was no Knit of his, and it was not a thing that should be repeated in the intents of the party. With regard to

HIS Wokx ON THE COUNCIL, he had done steryilitag hiS power for the count', and for the welfare of his towtl—(iipPliiiSi!)--hini if they thought fit to return him again he should pursue the same course he had previously. (Applause.)— Mr. Speakman then reviewed his work on the County Council. He claimed liat had he succeeded in getting the highway from the Halton boundary to the railway station declared a highway there would have been £2OO a year saved to the town, but another attempt, he said,, would be made. He had taken care to be placed upon the Committee of Technical Education in the interests of Runcorn, and the treasurer of Runcorn Commissioners now had something like £220 in his possession to be spent in the education of the youth of the town. At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Geo. Riggs, Ramford-st., was summoned for contraven- ing coal mine regulations. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared on behalf of Messrs. H chard Evans and Co., pro- prietors of the Ilavan nab Colliery, and stated that on the 27th January ow) of the firemen was directed to search the men as they went down to work in No. 2 pit; and among the men searched was the defendant. A tobacco pipe was found upon him and when asked if he had anything more he replied that he had not. The fireman, however, continued his search and found defendant had a lucifer match. It was of considerable importance that in mines where naked lights were not allowed to be used the men should not have in their possession either of the articles named, which might lead to a serious explosion.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.
DEATH OF MR. NATHANIEL ECKERSLEY.

The death is announc—e-d—oi-MTN—JlTE:leFickers- ley, DL., of Standish Hall, Wigan and Carlton Manor, Bradford, which took place on Monday, after a few weeks' illness at Standish Hall. Mr. Eckersley was deputy chairman of Parr's Banking Co., Limited, and he rarely failed to attend the annual and extraordinary meetings of the bank. He was one of the most prominent men in the history of the borough of. Wigan for the last half century. For forty years he was a member of the Wigan Corporation, on six occasions was elected ' Mayor, sat as member for the borough from 1866 to 11868 and from 1883 to 1885, retiring in the latter ' year owing to the borough losing one member under the redistribution scheme. He was the 'selected Conservative candidate for the Ince divi- sion, but afterwards 'retired from the position. Mr. Eckersley was seventy-six years old, and was highly respected by all classes for his geniality, liberality, and public spirit. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-7. and W. Durrox, Sankey-at.. Warrington.— Advt.

div.p: DONATION PROMICED BY M. BRUNNER

His attendances in the Council and its commit- tees were second in number only to the Chairman's, except latterly when his journey away had lost him two months. After referring to the main roads question, In- to which he said he should go further at another time; the speaker said the Runcorn Commissioners with Wid- nes Local Board had presented to Chester County Coun- cil through him and to the Lancashire County Council through Mr. Snape asking that an inquiry might be made as to a vehicular bridge spanning the Mersey adjoining the London and North-Western Railway. (Ap- planes.) He was proud to think that he was entrusted with the memorial and that he succeedml in carrying his motion for an inquiry by 45 votes to 15 and that Mr. Snape was also successful. He had no doubt that at no distant date they would have very satisfactory reports, as the bridge would prove a great public benefit. (Applause.) Mr. Kniveton said what he had stated on Wednesday he was prepared to say in Mr. Speakman's presence. He asked if Mr. Speakman would be prepared to vote for a motion having for its object the more

EQUITABLE TAXATION OF MANSIONS and parks, which were at the present time assessed at a ridiculous low sum. Whether he would vote for placing the taxation of ground rents on a more fair and equit- able basis, and whether supposing the question were brought before the County Council he would vote for the direct veto of the liquor trade in any shape or form. —Mr. Speakman replied that these questions did not come within the scope of the County Council at present and they did not know how they might turn up, but they might rely upon one thing, that what belonged to the Liberal party he should certainly vote for.—Mr. Temperlv said Mr. Speakman's

REPLY AS TO DIRECT VETO was not satisfactory.—Mr. Speakman said he could give no other under the circumstances.—Mr. Temperley said the licensing question was sure to come before the Council ia the next three years. Was Mr. Speakman prepared to support the direct vets no matter by whom brought in P—Mr. Speakman : Yes, of course, if it is brought in by the Liberal party I vote for it.—Mr. Tern- perley ; Not if it is brought in by a Tory ?—Mr. Speak- man replied in the affirmative.—Mr. Humphrey asked whether if the Liberal party voted against a vehicular bridge was Mr. Speakman going to support them. (Laughter.)—Mr. Clegg : I think it is too late to pro- pose
COMIC CONUNDRUMS.
(Laughter and applause.)—Mr. W. -Handley then sub- mitted a list of questions, including one whether the candidate would vote for the

MANAGEMENT OF TRH RIVER WEAVER being transferred and vested in the county council ? Mr. Speakman said he did not think he could be expected to answer all these questions straight away. With re- gard to the Weaver Trust, this question had been before the council, and it was decided technically that they could not take it over, but they had control over it so far that the accounts were audited and a proper state- ment submitted. The county did not want a white ele- phant at the present time. The funded debt of the trust was a quarter ot a million sterling. MR. OCKLESTON'S ADDRESS. Mr. Ocklestone, who was well received, then deli- vered an address. He said he was a Liberal, and the son of a Liberal, and he thought he should be a Liberal all his life, lie understood that they wished pi.m to come forward as a candidate for the Northern Division

of Runcorn in the Liberal interest. He should be very pleased to contest the Division as a Liberal, and as a Gladstonian-Liberal. (Applause.) He had only one leader—and that was that wonderful old man, Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) Be expressed his surprise that 15 Liberals voted against

THE VEHICULAR lIRIDGR. Re should be prepared to vote for the bridge independ- ent of politics. As to the other matters Mr. Handley had brought before their notice he should not like to make a definite and absolute promise until he had looked more carefully into them, but he thought they, were all things that he would vote for. In reply to Mr. Tensperley, Mr. Ockleston said he was
NOT A TEETOTALLER

but expressed himself in favour of local option. (Ap- plause.) In reply to Mr. Humphreys, Mr. Ockleston said he would refer to the compensation for extinct licenses question at some future time.—ln reply to Mr. Billington, he said he should be prepared to support Mr. Speakman in his efforts for

A TECHNICAL INSTITUTE. (Applause.)—Mr. T. Clegg moved that Mr. Speakman be the Liberal candidate for Runcorn South.—Mr. Jas. Lea seconded.—Mr. Kniveton moved an amendment, ex- pressing dissatisfaction at the manner in which Mr. Speakman had answered the questions, but it was not seconded.—Mr. A. Norman said he understood that it was a settled point that

MR. SAMUEL TAYLOR was coming out in Runcorn South and as there would thus be two Liberals he moved the Association take no part in that division, but leavl the matter in the hands of the electors.—The motion was seconded.—On a division

MR. SPEAKMAN WAS SELECTED by 25 votes to 4. A number of members did not vote.— Mr. Speakman, who had retired from the room, was called in and informed of his selection, and after some remarks by him, the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks having been accorded to the Chairman.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. At the fortnightly meeting of tne, above Order an essay was given by Mr. Joseph W. Boyle on "What is man ?" The writer dealt with the subject in a very able manner. He dilated on the physiological aspect of the question, explaining the structure of the human frame, the action of the heart, and the circulation of the blood. After the reading of the paper, there was a good discussion, in which the following members took part— Messrs. Edward Key, J. Clarke, John Jones, and Daniel Bisbrown. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to M. Boyle for his interesting paper. Mr. John Clarke occu- pied the chair. RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
