div.head: MR. SPEAKMADi BECOMF.S AN INDEPENDENT CANDIDATE.
div.p: MR. SPEAKMADi BECOMF.S AN INDEPENDENT CANDIDATE.

On Wednesday morning,Mr. W. Handley, secretary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association, received the following letter from Mr. Speakman :—" I regret very much to communicate to you, after a lapse of now nearly 30 years supporting of and working in the Liberal cause, that some of the loaders of the party should think fit to malign and libel me from time ts time. I did hope that my visit to the meeting on Saturday night would have brought harmony in our ranks ; it was hard to bear the onslaughts that were made upon me without the chance of reply at the close of the meeting. I feel it is due to those who kindly supported me to thank them for their confidence, which I do; but so long as Mr. Kniveton remains to disturb and annoy our party, I cannot remain longer in such association, and now beg respectfully to tender my resignation. There- fore, all that took place on Saturday night must, so far as I am concerned, be considered to be abrogated, and I intend to take my stand, as I did at the last election, on purely independent lines. From what has come to my knowledge, I am convinced that both at Wednesday night and Saturday night's meetings I was made the victim of a deeply laid scheme."

THE CONSERVATIVES AND THE SITUATION. A meeting of the Runcorn Executive of the Northwich Division Conservative Association was held on Monday evening in the Conservative Club, undar the presidency of Mr, John Meadowcroft. After a low,' deliberation the following resolution was passed, "That we consider politics foreign to the duties of the County Council, and that we decline to nominate a Conservative candidate as such, reserving to ourselves the right to consider future action as circumstances may determine." MR. HANDLEY'S REPLY TO MR. SPEAKMAN.

On receipt of the above communication Mr. W. Hand- ley, secretary to the Associati )n, sent the following reply:— "February 17, 1892. P. Speakman, Esq., C.C. Dear sir,—Owing to absence from home, I did not receive your letter until to-day, and the reading of its contents, I need not assure you, caused me great regret. The rules of the Association require the referring of resignations to the districts in which they occur ; I will, therefore, send on a copy of your letter to the district secretaries in order that they may submit it to the next district meet- ing. Faithfully yours, Wu. HANDLEY.
THE ADDRESSES.

As will be sean from our advertisinz columns, three of ' the gentlemen previously before the electors of Runcorn have issued addresses, and they will well repay perusal. Major Hazlehurst contests Runcorn North, as an inde- pendent, against Mr. W.Ockleston, the Liberal nominee. Mr. Philip Speakman offers himself to the electors of Runcorn South as an independent candidate, and it is generally understood that Mr. Samuel Taylor will be his 1 opponent, but that gentleman has not yet made a sign. The Conservatives are taking no official part. Mr. John Ashton magistrates' clerk, is the retiring officer. Friday next is the last day for nomination, and the election will take place on Saturday, March sth. Mr. E Wvnne Humphreys is acting as agent for Mr. Speak- man, and Mr. T. H. Annett is acting in a similar capa- city for Major Hazlehurst.
WIDNES.
It is highly improbable that there will be a contest in Widnes. It is fully expected that Alderman Snape and Councillor Snape will be returned unopposed.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN PUBLICAN. THE DISTURBED SUPPER PARTY.
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN PUBLICAN. THE DISTURBED SUPPER PARTY.

' At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Steele, James Woods, land- lord of the Bridge Inn, Ashbridge-st., Runcorn, was summoned on two informations for having on the 7th of February, kept open his premises for the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail to certain persons not bond fide travellers or persons lodging therein during the time the premises were required to be closed by law; also refusing 1:9 a ittcjCOnstablea who wgc qT.lMldflig to enter in the aeotitien of ; their duty.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys prosecuted for the police, and Mr. J. Harvey Simpson, of Man- Chester defended. From the statement of Mr. Humphreys, it appeared that at about 12.30 on the Sunday morning in question P.S. Gosling was on duty at the corner of Ash ridge-street and Lord-st., when he saw three men coming in the direction of the Bridge Inn. Opposite the entry that leads to the rear of the house he heard one man say " Come on ; let's have a drink." The reply was indistinguishable, but all the men went into the entry. A minute or two afterwards a man and a woman came down the street, and they also turned into the entry. Five minutes later the sergeant was joined by P.C. Hodgkinson, and together they went to the rear of the Inn. There was a light in the kitchen, and through the Venetian blind,which did not fit closely, the officers could see a portion of the room. Voices of men and women could be heard, and the sergeant heard a man's voice say "Let's have a hand at cards." Cards were brought out, and the officer heard a hand shuffled, and a man's voice then said " Here's good health." At this time P.C. tiodgkinson, who had gone to the front, was heard knocking at the principal door, and at once the light in the Vaults was turned out; but the door was not opened. The constable knocked for ten minutes at intervals of about 20 seconds. When the knocking com- menced the sergeant heard a woman say " Hush ! The police are at the front door let me have them there. and I will put them in a drawer where they would not find them." The sergeant then saw a woman place the cards in a drawer under some other things. Consider- able commotion ensued in the room, and the sergeant knocked at the back door, but got no reply, and heard the people trooping out of the kitchen, and the light waq lowered. The sergeant knocked again and the door was opened by Mrs. Woods, and he asked the defendant what men he had got in the place and the defendant replied " None," but a search revealed them in a sitting room upstairs, Kay said "We have been having a quiet evening by ourselves, and have been here all night, but we have had nothing to drink." The sergeant replied " I never said you had "and , he took the names and addresses of the men. On the counter in the bar were found a number of glasses and jugs newly washed.—T.S. Gosling corroborated these statements, and in cross-examination he said the men stopped till two o'clock. The defendant took the men to I the doctor to see if they were sober.—P.C. Hodgkinson corroborated, and said while the sergeant was upstairs Woods said "lam done this time."—For the defence Mr. Simpson said the defendant and the four men had spent the day in Liverpool at a football match and at the theatre, and they arrived home by the train reach- ing Runcorn at 12.15 midnight, and they were met at the Railway station by Mrs. Woods and her aunt, Mrs Beswick, who was staying with her for a few days. The railway porter, Walter Turner, would prove this. What therefore was more natural than that the defendants should ask the friends with whom he had spent the afternoon to come and have a little supper, especially as they were an well acquainted with Mrs.Beswick ? Although the police never saw any supper, a supper of sausages and mashed potatoes was i prepared and a portion of it was n the oven. He would prove that the knocking at the door was not heard; and persons talking in a room could not hear so much as a wasbecause no re theysn a person who was expecting a noise. Tliere why they should refuse to admit the police, would have to do sooner or later.—Mrs. Sarah Beswick, of 1131, Radnor-street, Hultne, Manchester, corroborated this statement. She said she only heard one knock. No cards were played or produced.—The men went upstairs after being in the kitchen a short time. She put the supper in the oven herself. She denied that the conversation described by the police took place. Mr. Woods invited the men to supper, principally to meet her, as she knew them all very well.—At this point of the case Mr. Reynolds was compelled to leave the court to keep an appointment, and the case was adjourned until Tuesday, when Mrs. Woods was called and contradicted the evidence of the prosecution. —Thomas Kay, of 27, Sutherland-st., Runcorn, gave evidence of the invitation, and said they went to four doctors afterwards because the sergeant said they had had enough to drink.—The defendant also gave a com- plete denial to the evidence of the prosecution, and stated that cards had never been played on his premises, and if Peter Smith said he had played cards with him on his own premises, it was a lie. The men had a drink to

r their supper at his expew.e.—Mr. Humphreys: Do yotz confine yourself to betting in this house ?—No I don't.— Is it not a fact that you continually use that house for betting purposes ?—Mr. Simpson strongly objected to these questions; they were an attempt to make Mr. Woods commit himself.—Mr. Humphreys repeated the question several times, but Mr. Simpson ordered his client not to answer, and the magistrates' clerk ruled that the questions should not be asked.—After a con- sultation in private, the Bench dismissed the case, and Superintendent Large then withdrew the case against the four men.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. T. Sutton Timmis. Present Major Wareing, Dr. O'keeffe, Dr. O'Donnell, Messrs. 11. Wade Deacon, B. Brown, S. Quinn, and G. H. Denby, clerk. The District Education Committee reported that during January 11 persons had made applications for the payment of school fees, 219 had been summoned for contravention of the Education Act, and five persons had been convicted by the magis trates. The Chairman of the Finance Committee (Major Wareing) submitted a statistical table giving the cost of teaching per head of children in average attendance during 1891. The net cost per head at Simmo Cross was 3s. Bd.; Warrington-road 10s. 10; and West Bank 9s. ; the net average being 6s. 11d., which repre- sented the sum that had to be paid out of the rates. The gross cost of teaching was £2 Is. lid. per head; this was without giving credit for any revenue. In 1885 the net cost was 3s. 54d. per head, as against 6s. lid. now, an increase of 100 per cent. The increase might be attributed to the additional cost of teaching, salaries having been increased year by year, and to additional expenditure in regard to the repair of buildings.—Mr. Brown remarked that the Committees ought to keep a watchful eye on the expenditure.—The Committee were thanked for preparing the statement.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT RUNCORN.

Thomas Scott, a Ship Canal employe, was sum- moned before Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting his wife, Ann Scott. Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the complainant and Mr. E. W. Ilumphreys for the defendant. The pro- secuting solicitor said the complainant lived in Fryer-st., where she kept a common lodging-house. The parties had been married four years, but had been separated on various occasions by mutual consent. He went away the first week in January, pro- mised never to return, and she gave him some money. On the Bth February he entered the yard of the house, and she asked him what he was doing there. He re- plied "I will soon show you," at the same time knocking her to the ground. She went into the house and he followed,and again struck her. For safety she went to a neighbour's, but returned in a quarter-of-an-hour, when the defendant pulled a red-hot poker from the fire and threatened to thrust it into her. A man who was pre- sent took the poker from him, and a fight between the two men ensued.—Mr. Lake said if their Worships were seisfied that the assault was of an aggravated character he should ask for a separation order.- -The Complainant corroborated this statement and in cross examination denied that she had committed adultery.—Other witnesses to the assault were called.— Mr. Humphreys said the defence was that the case was a tissue of lies from beginning to end, and that her con- duct with other men had given defendant great cause to , complain.—George Gilbert was called and stated that ' Mrs. Scott had told him that she was not married to Scott and she had promised to be with him more than once, and she had committed adultery with him.—By Mr. Lake: He had written letters to Mrs. Scott as Mrs. Nicheles and he told her husband about it.—Mr. Lake Are you not ashamed of yourself.—Witness : No.—Mr. Lake well you are a disgrace to manhood.—Witness said Mrs. Scott had summoned him for breaking the window of her house and he was sent to gaol for two months.— He had also been fined for assaulting her.—The Bench declined to grant the separation order but bound the defendant over to keep tke peace for six months himself in £5 and one surety in £lO.

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
ANNUAL TEA PARTY.

The annual tea party and entertainment in con- nection with Runcorn Co-operative and Industrial Society were held in the Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday evening, when about 500 persons sat down to an excellent tea. The good things were dispensed by the following ladies;---Miss Worthing- ton, Miss Smithem, Mrs. Evans, Mrs. Street, Miss Hassey, Mrs. Clark, Mrs. Rogerson, Mrs. Pendle- bury, Mrs, Francis, Kn. Evans, Miss Williams, Mrs. T. Cropper (Liverpool), Mrs. Wm. Cropper (Liver- pool), Mrs. Curzon, Mrs. Price, Mrs. Baxter, Mrs. Randles, Mrs. Leach, Mrs. Findlay,Mrs. Davies, Mrs. Silitoe, Mrs. Woods, Mrs. Johnson, Mrs. Richardson, Mrs. Lowe, Mrs. Betley, Mrs. Broady, Mrs. Carter, &c. A large and appreciative audience assembled for the concert, which was presided over by Mr. Daniel Worthington, who in the course of a capital speech, congratulated the members upon the success of their business during the past year. The sales haj. amounted to ..£77,000, and the profits to £11,36g. This profit had been realised without any effort on their part beyond purchasing their goods at their own stores, and they had all participated in the benefits to be thus derived. He touched upon the im- portant results that accrued through having all this money distributed amongst them. He remarked that the society had during the year advanced £2,000 on mortgage, and he congratulated those members who under the operation of this new rule had become their own landlords. They had the large sum of about £13,000 lin the bank,and he urged the members to take advent- ' age of the easy terms olltied members to become owned of their own houses, so that the money would be profit- able to them and to the Society.—The programme was then proceeded with. A glee party rendered "Let the hills resound with sound," with good effect, and Mr. John Betney sang "The Wolf," with power and expres- sion. The duet "The Gipsy Countess," by Miss John- son and Mr. Leathwood received a well merited encore and Mr. Shingler gave a very good rendition of " The storm fiend." Later the same gentleman sang" Four jolley smiths." " Killarney " was sung in charming style by Miss Johnson, and Mr. Sanders's recitation of " The Quack Doctor" provoked much merriment. Mr. Lacy sang "The Pilgrim of love " and " 'the thorn" appropriately, and Mr. Leathwood gave "Anchored" in a manner that was highly appreciated. Miss Newell sang "The song that reached my heart" in nice style. A vociferous encore rewarded Mr.Holroyd for his singing of "Barney take me home again," and a similar compliment was paid to Messrs. Cropper and Withington for thelt fez- , dering of "By-and-Bye," in which they introduced local hits which convulsed the audience, with laughter. Mr. Vf ithincton also sang two comic songs, which were enthu„ siastically encored. Miss Rogers was applauded for singing "Lily Dale," and a pleasant and enjoyable even- ing was brought to a close by the glee party singing "All among the barley." The customary votes of thanks were passed during the evening.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

AN OBSTREPEROUS MENDICANT CRIPPLE. Thomas Johnson, a collier, of 37, Scotland-road, was charged before the Warrington magistrates at the police court on Monday, with being diunk and disorderly in tiolden-square on Saturday night. P.S. Cheeney said the prisoner was drunk, exhibiting the stump of his arm to people in the street. He had a candle in his hand, and was asking for alms, and because they would not give hina anything called them " all the names he could lay his tongue to." As witness took him to the police station, he abused him shamefully all the way. The pri- soner was sent to jail for seven days, with hard labour. TREE CHARGE OF CRUELTY TO CHILDREN.

Thos. and Charlotte Sidebotham who were charged eight weeks previously with cruelly neglecting their children, were brought up on remand at the borough magistrates' court, on Monday. Mr. Shearer appeared an behalf of the Board of Guardians, who had conducted the prosecution, and stated that the children had been in the Workhouse in the meantime; and they were now brought forward to show that they were considerably improved.—lnspector Bowen said there was a great improvement, too in the defendant's house, and they had provided plenty of bedding.—Both of them expressed their regret for their conduct, the husband stating that the cause was his having been out of employment, but that he had now obtained some; and the wife promised that the children should never be negleeted in future. Mr. Shearer withdrew the summonses, and it *as agreed that the parents should reinove the children from the Workhouse in a week.

div.head: SEC/ZINO IN A MINE.
div.p: SEC/ZINO IN A MINE.

At the Newton Petty 'Sessions, 3n Saturday, Michael Walsh, furnaceman, was charged with having in his cos.session a pipe and tobacco for smoking in Edge Green miae, Golborne, on the 14th ult. Mr. Stuart, solicitor, appeared for the prosecution on behalf of Messrs. R. Evans and Co., proprietors of the mine. He stated that on the date mentioned the underlooker went with another man to see the defendant. He sent the other man away, and hid himself The defendant looked carefully round to see if anybody Was there, but did not know the underlooker was concealed. He then pulled out a pipe and lit it at the furnace, and coin- menced to smoke. The underlooker at once came to

him, took his pipe from him, and reported the matter. The mine wee a fiery one, and there had been accidents therein times past. Colonel McCorquodale and Mr. Gil- leeole did not take [mit in the hearing of the case, being interested parties.—The defendant was fined 103. and coats.

div.head: RAILWAY STATION THIBF.
div.p: A RAILWAY STATION THIBF.

At the Borough magistrates' court,on Wednesday morn- ing, Elijah Ilillma.n, glass maker, of 202 Longford-st., was charged with stealing from the waiting room at Bank Quay Station, on the previous afternoon, a parcel of Railway Guides and two posters, value is. the prop- erty of the London and North Western Railway Co., also with assaulting James Whittaker, porter employed at the station. From the evidence of Mr. Ashurst, station- master, Joseph Whittaker, Edward Clarke, clerk in the booking office, William Booth, and a police constable the following appeared to be the facts :—He had been in the habit of hanging about the station, and several articles had been missed, and on the afternoon in question he was seen looking suspiciously into the waiting rooms. A " test parcel" of the nature described was made up, and was placed in the first class waiting room, and marked" T. Jones, Samples." The prisoner went into the waiting room, sat down and warmed his hands, came out and went in again, and was seen from a van stand- ing opposite the door, to put the parcel under his coat. He was followed by Whittaker, and overtaken and seized by him beside the park railings. He struggled violently and bit Whittaker, and one of the company's men, who lived near, had to be brought to assist him in getting the prisoner to the police station. Ile pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to a month's hard labour. BOYS ON STRIKE. At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, four lads named John Wright, Thomas Grimes, James Coin, and Geo. Bailey, were charged with assaulting another lad named Edgar Taylor on the 9th February. Mr. Browne said he appeared on behalf of Messrs. Robinson, Son, and Skinner, in whose employ Taylor was. The . .

case was really one of intimidatio'n on account of a strike at the works. There were 22 lads who went out , on strike on the Monday afternoon previous.and stopped , the whole works for a day and a half. Mesers. Robin- son, Son, and Skinner, employed other boys to take their places, and one. Edgar Taylor, was sent out on an errand, at half-past three on Tuesday afternoon. These four boys waylaid him, kicked him, and struck him. Edgar Taylor said he was 14 years of age, and was en- gaged at "Messrs. Robinson's on Tuesday afternoon. He went out on an erran 1, and walked down Factory-lane. The lads were there, and they attacked him. Bailey struck him first, but he could not say who kicked him. He knew all the lads. Edwin Armstrong said he noticed the lads hanging about the works. Wean the lad Tay- lor came back, he looked as if he had been assaulted. George Lewis, a lad, said that he had been sent out on an errand on the day mentioned, and Bailey ran him back into the works four times. Alderman Chandley said the conduct of the lads was impudent. It was wrong of them to g 0 on strike and then to try to prevent others working. They would each !se bound over in £5 to keep the peace for six months. • : CHARMS OF CRIMINAL ASSAULT. At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Chandley (chairman), Md. Sutton, Councillor James Fairclough, and Captain Ridg- way, John Wm. Sykes, 6, Green-st., Thomas Bennett, 6, Dale-st., Sankey Bridges, and Wm. Threadgold, 54, Wil- derspool-road, all employed by the London Boot Re- pairing Co., Liverpool-rd., were brought up on remand from Monday, charged with having on the 20th ult., at their employers' premises, committed a criminal assault upon Mary Yates,aged 22 years,a young woman of weak intellect, and the unmarried stepdaughter of James McNallum, 51, Howard-street, Sankey Bridges. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution on be- half of Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, and in consequence of that gentleman's illness ; and stated that being a member of the Town Council, lie charged nothing, for his services. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the defence. Evidence was given by the complainant, her mother, Dr. Adams, and Detective-Sereeant Monaghan, and, accord- ing to the last-named, on his apprehending the prisoners under warrant, they made a statement to the effect that the complainant was a consenting, in fact a requesting, party. The prisoners were committed for trial to the Liverpool Assizes, bail being allowed in two sureties of £25 each.

----• ASSAULT ON THE NUISANCES INSPECT.R. At the Warrington Magistrates' Court,on Nlnnday,Peter Robinson, 20, Church-st., was charged with assaulting Ralph Norman, Inspector of Nuisances, on the Bth inst.— Mr. Browne defended.—The complainant said on Monday aftornoon, the cl-lendant stopped him in Battermarket- street, and said "Oh, I want you," and got hold of him, and said" Have you ever committed perjury ?"—He replied" No."—The defendant said "Are you sere you did not do it in tho County Court ?"—He again replied " No.—" Nor in tho Police Court ?" continued the de- fendant.—" No." again answered witness. He added he did not want to be detained there by a drunkeelliani and wrested himself away. Robinson gc,t hold otjiim again, and he wrested himself away a second thnei.'''The man followed him down the street, and used disvriceful •language, and said with an oath he had told Alderman' Francomb about his games and he was going to watch

him. The defendant attracted everybody's attention. HE followed him down to Orford-street end and down Church-st., conducting himself is a most abominable manner.—Mr. Scotson correborated.—Mr. Browne said his client protested that he had not used any bad lan- guage, but he had taken more whisky than was good for him on account of influenza. He thought if he was bound over that would meet the justice of the case.—Alderman Francomb said he was sure from what he knew of the defendant he would not have conducted himself so had he not been in drink.—He was bound over in the sum of £5 for six months, and ordered to pay the costs.

div.head: NEGLECT OF CHILDRHX.
div.p: NEGLECT OF CHILDRHX.

At the Borough-Vagi;tl;te;-Co—n-rt-,.. -yesterday, Mary Turner, St. Mary-st., Latchford, was charged with wil- fully neglecting her children Mary Jane, Wm. and James Turner, in such a manner, as was likely to cause injury to their health. Mr. B. Shearer, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Board of Guardians.—He said the defen- dant was the wife of James Turner, a ship canal labourer who was in receipt of £3 a week wages. He visited their house a fortnight, that day since, at 21 minutes to 12 in the morning and there found the three children. who had not tasted food that day. Another child had gone to school without breakfast. He understood that the defendant's husband was a very respectable indus- trious man, so much so that the Guardians had decided not to proceed against him. He left his wife in the morning with the children, and as soon as he turned his back she went off. They lived in a large house, fairly furnished. The youngest child was only 18 months old, and was suffering from whooping cough on the day in question.—Annie Maria Rough, said her husband was employed on the Ship Canal, and paid to defendant's husband £3 a week. Witness lived next door, and de- posed to the neglect of the children, and said she had complained to the police about it. The defendant, however, was a good wife, and mother if she would only keep from drink, and had promised and tried hard to do so.—Detective-sergeant Monaghan said there was a great improvement both in the children and the state of the house.—The defendant had been previously before the court for being drunk, and the Chairman told her that the case was a sorrowful one, and nothing would bring down severer punishment upon parents than subjecting their children to hardships. She promised to take the I pledge, and was fined 10s, and costs, £1 in all.—John Coatley, labourer, 6, Tilley-street, was charged with a like offence in the cases of four young children. Mr. Shearer was prosecuter on behalf of the Guardians. He said the neglect of the children had been going on for some time, and lie would like to hays the case adjourned in order to have the defendant's wife in the dock. She was in jail out would come out on March 2nd.—Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, deposed to finding the children at home in a neglected state on the 4th inst., the father who had been at work during the night, being in bed. There was food on the table, and the eldest girl was toasting bread. He noticed a pecu- liar starved expression on the faces particularly of two of the children. The father blamed the mother. Wit- ness found that on many occasions the children hod been ill-treated by the parents; and pointed to a poker on the court table, with which he said one of the children, a younger child had been beaten. Themother is a very drunken woman. Two of the children,girls, were brought forward, and the junior orte said she had been beaten by her mother with the poker more than once for not telling her father who had been in,but he had never beaten her. She said she had had enough to eat, and had been washed daily and went to school and was in the second standard.—Mr. Shearer said the defendant had been up for being drunk.—The case was adjourned for 14 days ' for the wife to be brought up.

TRAVELLING Wrrnotrr a TlCEET.—William Wardle was charged with riding on the Cheshire Lines Railway, from Liverpool to Warrington. on the previous Friday eveninT, without a ticket.—A ticket collector said that his atten- tion was drawn by a passenger to the man, lying under the seat of the carriage. lie was pulled out, and it was found that he had no ticket. lie was taken to the bride- well.—Prisonet was ordered to pay 10s, and costs, or 14 days' impriscnment with hard labour. BREACH OF THE SANITARY LAWS.—Rosanna Seutla- cott, a Staffordshire woman, of 76, Church-at., was charged with discharging certain utensils into an aslipit there on the 9th inst., contrary to tho bye-laws of the borough.—lnspector Norman proved the ease, and said that the practice he complained of was not only a nuis- ance, but the contents of the ashpit were made useless for conversion at the depot.—She was exceedingly voluble in her own defence, and said she did not know she was doing wrong and said there ought to be more bills posted so that people could be warned.—Alderman Francomb You don't want him to have one posted on his back,and come and stand before rm.—Site was fined ss. including costs.

PEENS AND DlBOR.DlDlLL—George.Whitfield,drunk on the Bth inst., at Sankey Bridges, was fined 2s.' ed. and costs.—James Daniels, Ship Canal labourer, drunk and disorderly on the Bth inst., was fined ss.—Robert Whit- field, at Poulton, on the 18th inst.,los. and costs.--Jos. ing infringements penalized the Recs, on two occasions, but nothing came of Turner's kicks. Thorniley and Buckley were prominent in some loose play, but Seddon punting along touch landed the oval near the half-way. Some sharp passing saw Potts making headway along the popular side, his progress being stayed after a run of fifteen yards. Another free kick fell to Warrington, and Turner essayed another shot at goal, with a futile result. His forwards followed up well, and Buckley was all but a scorer when Jackson nipped the oval from his feet, and a ponderous kick landed the ball at neutral territory. , Webster now had a vast amount of work to do, and a short punt and quick following up sent the oval near the r line, Seddon throwing into touch-in-goal. From the scrimmage ordered near the posts, Warrington were I penalized, mad Dolan and Brears supplementing the kick with a fine dribble, Evaas fielded the oval well, and play was confined to centre-field. By degrees the ball was taken to the Warrington line, and a series of stiff scrim- mages was at last relieved when Tears got away from tha nick, but his pass was a shade wrong. Another passing bout by Bate, Antrobus, and Webster saw the three-quarters slipping intro touch, and thea Bate (St. Helens) tackled Antrobus near his quarter flag. Handles was next penalized, but Seddon's shot came to nought, and some fine forward play by Davies, Turner, Ashton, and Knowles rushed the oval down the popular side, only to find Jackson responding in true style. Evans was all there, and a grand run right into his opponents' quarters elicited cheers. from both sides. The play was again driven back to the visitors' quarter flag, and Turner was much en evidence when he followed and tackled Seddon. A pretty run by Potts was negatived by Seddon, and another bout of passing, initiated by Bate, landed the visitors once more on the aggressive. Briars soon had the oval at the Warrington quarter flag, when Potts dribbled out of danger, and half-time was signalled with no substantial score. Webster foiled any response to the I kick-off, whilst Antrobus was a shade too slow in tak- ing advantage of a pass from his companion half. The next item of interest was some splendid combination between Bate, Heesom, and Potts. The former had got clear from a scrimmage, and passed to Heesom, who transferred to Potts, but as the latter was in the act of grounding, he was tackled before accomplishing his object, and carried back into play. Succeeding this hard lines came a vigorous attack on the Warrington goal, but Evans was particularly safe. The rest of the game was of a give-and-take nature, free kicks chiefly to Warrington monopolizing the attention. On one occasion Turner got clear, and Potts was held near the line again. With two minors only registered, a draw was the result, but Warrington must be considered a trifle unlucky in not reversing their first defeat of a goal to a try.

Teanis :—Warrington : J. W. Evans, back ; H. Webs- ter, F. Heesom, and E. Potts, three-quarter backs ; John Bate and W. Antrobus, half backs ; H. Ashton. Fair. Turner, V. Handles, T. Donohue, H. Tears, J. T. Thornily, J. Knowles, T. Davies, and J. Buckley, for- wards. St. Helens Recs. : Jackson, back; Ellison, Uns- worth, and Seddon, three-quarter backs ; Joseph Bate and Turton, half backs; Dolan, Fildes, Mounsey, Parr, Briars, Anderton, Chapman, Reynolds, and Doherty, forwards.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday miust be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wedueeday morning.
RUGBY.

ST. ILEUMS ROVERS v. LATCHFORD RECRRATION.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Satur- day afternoon. Final result—Latchford Recreation 7 minors, St. Helens Rovers 5 minors. WARRINGTON" A "v. ST. FIBLENS RECREATION "A."— The home team was severely crippled in having nine of their usual 15 absent, in the above match, played at Warrington. Having won the toss,the visitors decided to have the sun at their backs,and with Warburton kicking off, the contest started. There was nettling very brilli- ant in the style of the combatants, though the Recs. forced Warrington on their lines, but after a sharp scrummage, Ashurst, by a punt, made matters more even. Laws, of Cleckheaton fame, hereabouts tried a drop at goal, but Hamblett returned the leather. Hamp- son, Forster, Barnes, J. Warburton, and Lingard, fol- lowed up this advantage by a loose dribble, and from Lally's pass Chappell forced a minor. Westall and Chappell were next prominent, and a bout of passing between Little, Bolton, and Eves was spoiled by the over zeal exhibited by the visitors. This was succeeded by Lally and Lawless by their smartness gaining a lot of ground, and Chappell, passing to Westall, the latter ran close to the line before being stopped. A kick by 801-1 ton was then mulled, allowingtlae Recs. to get a foothold in Warrington quarters. Some very fine kicks between' Vfestall, Lawless, and Laws ended advantageously to the home team, but directly afterwards the last-named found touch inside his opponents' 25. A capital relief by Russell, Bailey, W. Warburton, and Hampeon, sent the oval to more desirable quarters, and Lally and War- burton by kicks forced the Recs. on their lines, the whistle blowing for half time with nothing scored. Upon the resumption of hostilities the Saints carried the war- fare right to the line, until Hampson effected relief. A ' screw kick by Ashurst was badly mulled, only: to see Laws save the danger. Warburton, Forster, Lingard, and Wilkins, were hereabouts notable, and another kick' by Ashurst found the combatants vieing with one another at the visitors 25. Lally then had the hardest of hard lines, as after having a try under the posts at his mercy, he stumbled, and the chance was lost, the Recs. kicking dead. Another grand bit of play by Lally followed, and passing to Ashurst the latter was only pulled up on the line. Ultimately Mees put in a long kick, and the home custodian mulling, the Recs. were placed on side and scored an easy try, from which a goal was kicked. Warrington attacked vigorously after this but the effort came too late, and Warrington retired defeated by 1-0-0 to 0-0-3.

div.head: BRADFORD V. RUNCORN.
div.p: BRADFORD V. RUNCORN.

Played at Runcorn on Saturday in spring-like weather. The match had created a vast amount of interest from the fact that some weeks ago the teams played a drawn game at Bradford. The homesters had a powerful team up, but unfortunately the visitms had only two of their regular backs available, and neither Briggs nor Emmett, the international half backs, turned out. Hawcridge also had not sufficiently recovered from his recent attack of influenza to enable him to captain thw Yorkshire-men. Toothill commexcad hostilities at 3.30, a return being made to half-way by Peudlebury. Fielden put in a long punt, which Houghton returned with interest. Toothil' started a nice passing movement, but after the ball had exchanged hands several times Richards spoiled a certain score by knocking on. The Runcorn forwards rushed the ball to the centre, where the game was spiritedly contested. Abrams punted into touch. Jenkinson was instrumental in removing the game, but Houghton was twice applauded for his effective kicking when severely pressed. Riley dribbled close on to the Bradford line, but Dewhurst, Richards and roothill again carried the game to neutral territory. The game was contested in a very spirited manner, being of a most open character, .and the ball travelled quickly about the field. For a time Runcorn had the best of matters. Pendlebury spoiling a chance of scoring by passing forward. Hough- ton returned a long kick by Jenkinson with interest,and the homesters continued to have the best of it. Fielden next essayed a run, but was promptly col- , lared. Abrams received and made oll' at top speed,l but passed forward when a try seemed certain. Scrim- maging ensuing in Bradford quarters, the visiting for- wards, led by Fisher and Toothill, removed tho game once again to the hilf-way line, where some smart play was witnessed. Pefilleburr collared Fielden grandly, just as the latter was about to put his foot to the leather, but a moment later the Bradfordian was cheered for a grand run. Abrams picked up from scrimmage and paPsed to Crompton, who gave to Davies, the latter punting splendidly into touch at the Bradford quarter flag. Exchanges between Runcorn backs was next wit- nessed, but Crompton held the ball too long, and was collared. The game still continued of a ding-dong character, and the homesters in particular displayed brilliant form, and treated the spectators, of whom there were some 6,000 present,tosome splendid sequences of passing. Doyle missed hie kick, and Abrams threw to' Crompton, who scored a magnificent try behind the posts, the same player piloting the oval over the cross- bar amidst frantic cheers. After the restart from centre, Duckett, a Bradford half, was injured and had to retire. Runcorn, spurred on by their success, played for all they were worth and kept Bradford continually on the defensive. Hughes made his mark for a free kick and Houghton made a good attempt for goal from half-way. Flail-time score t—Runcorn 1 goal, Bradford nil. Faulkner re-started, Jenkinson punting back to c an tre, where for some minutes hostilities were located. Abrams put in some grand foot work,which carried play close to the Bradford line. Duckett, who had re-started after the interval, was again compelled to retire. As a reoult of grand passing, Crompton secured and dropped a magnificent goal. Following this, Bradford asserted their superiority, and Doyle and Wright were the chief means of the visitors getting close to the Runcorn line. A dead ball accruing from a shy for goal, passing be- tween Wright,Doyle,and Fielden gave the latter a chance but Pendlebury hauled the Bradfordian down before he fairly got under way. Jenkins had his kick charged,and Abrams picked up, being collared, however, just outside the coveted line. At this period Crompton received a fracture to his shoulder, which necessitated his leaving the field, and just afterwards Duckett made a further effort to assist his comrades. The game up to this period had been of a most exciting character, though Runcorn had considerably the best of matters, and after severe pressure, Massey scored, which was not improved upon, Faulkner failing to place the ball between the posts. Final result.—Runcorn 2 pals 1 try (11 points) Bradford 3 minors (nil). WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RECREATI ON,

The Warringtonians journeyed to St. Het .ns, on Saturday, where the Recreation Club were met in the return engagement. The Warrington team differed from that originally chosen, the services of "Smack " Bate being required in bringing about the downfall of the Midland Counties at Whalley Range, whilst the indisposi- tion of Boscow at back, caused Evans to vacate his post at three-quarter, letting in Potts, a player who did justice to his selection. Fully 700 took advantage of the special train run to the glass-blowing town, and the day being beautifully fine, everything pointed to a good, though stubborn, contest.

winning the toss, the visitors had the advantage of the slight incline, and Seddon kicking off, Handles mulled the return, and Warrington were forced to scrimmage near their 25 flag. An infringement by the home half backs gave Warrington relief, and following up the advantage, Antrobus dribbled through Use ruck and took the oval beyond the Recs.' quarter flag. Here Turner, Ashton, and Knowles were busy in their endeavours, whilst the attempts of Seddon, Ellison, and Unsworth to

clear were frustrated by the accurate tackling of the opposing three-quarters. Free kieks were freely appealed for, and as freely given, and for fully ten minutes the game was a monotonous aeries of exchanges relieved by play of a loose scrambling order. Play was located dangerously near the Saints' posts, when Elison cleared well, and Evans was in turn called upon, a big response being forthcoming. Still Warrington pursued the aggressive, and the homsters had an anxious rime of ' it when John Bate, Heesom, Turner arid Webster passed, the latter being tackled not a moment too soon. Eventually the home forwards rushed down the popular side, and the oval was sent dad. Turner'sdrio • ant was seconded by Potts meeting Jackson's reply, and againthe siege was raised. Randles spoiled Unsworth, and the oval was about to betaken over when Seddon nipped tIP, and a lucky clear staved off the well-meant attempt. The Warrington half backs passed well to each other, and on fleesom receiving he was about to part to Webster when he was firmly grassed by 13rears and Dolan. War.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION RRSIIRTR T. GRAILIIAIS ScHooL.—This match was played on Saturday, and the Reserve had to put up with another defeat. Jones was kept busy in goal, but the grand piay of the home team was far too much for the Reserve,lsherwood,Francomb, Fennelly, and Reed, played a good game for the scholars, and Cornforth, Mather, Jones, Brookes, and Newton played well for the Reserve. Final seer@ : Grammer School five goals, Reserve nil. Isherwood kicked four of the goals, and Fennelly put in the fifth. WARRINGTON Sr. ELFIN:I'S T. C. ONIONS' "CHASE—This match was played on the Saints' ground, Dalton Bank, on Saturday. The visitors were composed of players , from district clubs, including Orford Barracks, Stockton ' Heath, and several players from Warrington Association, owing to their match being cancelled. St. Elphin's kicked off, and at once attacked, but after exchange kicks play s•ttled in the home half. Cooke relieved with a huge kick, Tickle returning nicely, and the visitors looked like scoring, but several poor attempts to score were made. Several corners were forced, but the defence of tho home team was admirable. Turner and Hatton then got possession, and took the ball to the visitors' goal, and after several futile attempts, Hatton scored with a splendid shot from the left. Half time ai•rived, the Saints leading by one to none. The visitors started with a rush, but S. Elphircs played up well, and again attacked their opponents' goal. Several good attempts were made, and Turner scored, with a low shot. This seemed to rouse the visitors, and they brought the leather close to the home lines. Clayton took a corner kick, from which a lightning shot was put into goal. Chantler hit the ball with his knee, and was charged before he could return, but he threw out whilst on the ground, and Piicenix kicked over the line. The visitors still kept up the pressure, certainly deserving better luck, but play was in midfield when time arrived, and St. Elphin's had won a good gains by two goals to none.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

At a meeting of the Yorkshire Union,held at Leeds, on Monday night, the following were chosen to represent Yorkshire against England at Leeds on Saturday next: —Goldthorpe (Hunslet), back; Dyson (Huddersfield), Lockwood (fieckmondwike), and Summersgill (Leeds), three-quarter backs ; Briggs (Bradford), and Varley Litersedge), half backs ; Bromet (Taticaster, captain), Toothill (Bradford), Bradshaw (Cr:alley), De whurst ( Bradford), Broadley (Bingley),Xicol (Brighouse), Wood (Brighouse), Bethnal' (Manningliain), and Jowett (Heck- mondwike), forwards.

Several causeg served to diminish the interest in the appearance of the Midland Counties at Whalley Hangs on Saturday. First, they came without several of their best men—Evershed and Percival among the number,— and then it was known that the issue could not affect the question of championship. Lancashire were also only moderately represented, Marsh, Sullen, and ryke being unavailable. The changes did not strengthen the team, and until the last quarter of an hour or so the play of the Lancastrians was disappointing. They ought to have won in much more decisive fashion than by two tries, and it would have gone hard with them had the visitors turned up in full force. Their efforts lacked finish, and at times combination was entirely. wanting.

Bate, of Warrington, was certainly the most effective man on the Lancashire side, He completely outshone not only Cross, his fellow half-back, but also the half-backs on the other side. The style in which he dodged and Wooled his opponents was a treat to see, and he was instrumental in getting the first try by handing over the ball to Valentine after practically all opposition had been passed.

Some disappointment has been caused in Warrington in consequence of " Smack " Bate having been passed over in the selection of half-backs to play for the Rest of England against Yorkshire. It was thought that after the splendid play he has shown in county matclens, and especially on Saturday against the Midland countie. his claims could not very easily be overlooked. It is sometimes suspected that the selections for these coveted positions are not always altogether decided by merit on the football field, arid when we see that a " De Winton " from the swell Illarkheath Club is to be Taylor's compan- ion at half-back, oue Can hardly be less suspicious on that account.

At a meeting of the county committee, held in Man- chester on Thursday night, Brennan, the Widnes captain, was suspended for a month. In a match last Saturday aaaiost Aspull the Widnes players diAputed a decision of the referee, Mr. Slevin, Of Wigan, and left the field. Brennan took the whole of the responsibility of this action upon himself, and suffers the sentence named. Had he net done so the club itself would most probably have been severely dealt with.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

-------•• Preston North End, the only Lancashire team which survived the second round of the competition for the Football Association Challenge Cup, suffered defeat from Notts Forest, on Saturday, and as a consequence there will, for the first time fcr ten years, be no representa- tives of that famous football district in the semi-final stage of the competition. The disasters of Lancashire have been the triumphs of the Midlands. Aston Villa, West Bromwich Albion, and Notts Forest—the three clubs which have qualified for the semi-final ties—all belong to the Midlands, whilst. the right to the fOurth place has still to be fought out between Stoke and Sun- derland, two hours' play between these elevens on Saturday having failed to settle the question of supre- macy. As the match will have te be replaved'at Sunder- land, Stoke, despite the pluck and determination they have displayed in the two latest rounds, will scarcely be expected to make further progress in the competition, but they may be heartily congratulated upon what they have already done.

Of the clubs left in the contest, both Aston Villa and West Bromwich Albion have previously secured final honours at Kensington Oval, but several years elapqed since Notts Forest acquitted themselves so briliimntly as they have done this winter. In the North the Sunderleuu tam—cornposed almost exclusively of Sc‘dclimen—are expected to.tnake a bold hid for posses- sion of the Cup; but it will be strange indeed if the Mid- lands. with three places in the last four,lail to carry off the national trophy.

div.p: A RUNCORN COMMISSIONER CHARGED WITH ASSAULT.

Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Steele, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Peter Smith, Chemist and Druggist, was summoned for assaulting his wife Mary Ann Smith.—Mr. Murphy, of Liverpool, represented the complainant. The defendant did not appear.—The magistrates' clerk (Mr. Ashton) had received the following telegram handed in at Wavertree-road Post Office, Liverpool :—" Smith's unable to leave his bed the last ten days. Ask for further adjournment of a week, Glew."—Mr. Murphy asked for a warrant that this man might be made to attend to the summons because he did not think he was treating the Bench with respect or fair- ness to any solicitor. The case had been adjourned once for the defendant's convenience and his obvious duty was to communicate with his solicitor who would have been quite ready to communicate with him, but he had neither taken that course, nor the usual proceeding of sending a doctor's certificate. He had seen the defend- ant's solicitor and while he would not say what the soli- citor told him privately, he might state that the relations between solicitor and client were uwatisfactory.—P.S. Woolley proved the service of the summons.—Mrs. Smith, examined by Mr. Murphy, said her husband assaultea her on the 28th January in the early morning. He caused her head to bleed and she was bruised about/ the head and body.—The Bench granted the warrant. On Monday night Mr. Smith who had eluded the Live- rpool detectives gave himself up at the Runcorn Police Station and he was brought beforee Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Stub. Mr. Burton acted for the defendant.—Mr. Murphy said subject to an expression which he under- stood his friend was ready to make, he thought their worships might be relieved from the trouble of investi- gating this matter.—Mr. Burton said Mr. Smith desired that no reflection should be made upon his wife with reference to her conduct in those proceedings or in any other matter whatever.—Mr. Reynolds : There has been none.—Mr. Murphy ilot in this court, but it is under- stood that the defendant had allowed words to escape him of an unsatisfactory character, and from which Mrs. Smith felt bound to vindicate herself in every way. Therefore after hearing that explanation I am only too happy to be able to withdraw the charge.— The Clerk : I understand there has been some statement made outside.—Mr. Burton : And which I desire upon behalf of the defendant to withdraw,—Mr. Reynolds : With which we have nothing to do. It is a matter be- tween man and wife, and I should think to withdraw was the most sensible course.—The charge was then withdrawn, and the defendant was liberated.
MEETING OF TANNERS AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday night, a meeting of tanners was held in the large room adjoining the Seven Stars Inn, Bridge-street, for the purpose of hearing an address by Mr. 11. Preece, of Loncl,ln, secretary to the Amalgamated Leather Trade Union. Mr. J. Price, president of the Warrington Trades Council, and secretary of the local branch of the Navvies' and General Labourers' Union, occupied the chair, and there were also present, in addition to Mr. Preece, Mr. .T. Waring, secretary to the Warrington branch of the Leather Trade Union, Mr. W. H. Bullock, secretary to the Warrington Trades Council, and Mr. T. B. Malkin, secretary to the Warrington Ironworkers' Union. There was only a small attendance.

The CHAIRMAN addressed the meeting, in the course of his observations stating that he did not know that he ever came across a trade which worked for a Ir.wer wage than that of the tan- ners. He urged that there should be direct labour representation in Parliament to remedy such grievances. Lie referred to a question that had been put to him as to whether trades unions were driving all the trade out of the country, his answer having been that it was such abuses as the heavy royalties paid to individuals on the mining industry that were doing this. These, he main- tained, should be much smaller and should be paid to tho State. _ _

...„ ........ Mr. PRIIIICH then spoke. He said he had just returned from a trip to Scotland where—in Glasgow—a reduc- tion of the wages of the tanners of d. per hide, or es. to 7s. per week per man had taken place. After prepar- ing the way by correspondence, he had gone there with the object of animating them to a determined resist- ance to the reduction, but on hie reaching Glasgow he was mortified to find that the men had accepted the masters' terms. He had, however, devoted himself to forming branches of the Leather Trade Union in Scot- land, to be prepared for such emergencies in future. He asserted that such a reduction in wages in the trade there would be sure to be followed by a reduction throughout the United Kingdom ; and if the tanners'of Warrineton did not take care to be combined against it they would find themselves in the same position as those in Glasgow. Their labour was their only stock in trade, and it was their duty to sell it as dearly as they could. The leather trade had not taken advantage of trades unionism in order to place itself on a footing with other trades, but he believed it would be recognised by the Labour Commission, before which he intended to giro evidence on its behalf. It was for the Warrington tan- ners to take advantage of unionism to bring their wages up to the standard of those paid in the south. Mr. Preece strongly endorsed the remarks of the Chairman on the subject of mining royalties. The CKAIRMAN and Mr. MALKIN addressed some fur- ther remarks to thelnecting, after which, Mr. Bottoot moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Preece. Mr. WARING seconded. He said working 14 to 16 hours a day for employers was ruining the cause of the tanners both in Warrington and Glasgow. (A Voice : "24 hours, more like.") The tanners would never im- prove their condition until they put an tnd to the sys- tem of overtime. (Applause.) The vote was carried, and Mr. Preece thanked the meeting, which concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.p: Ettters to tin attor.
THE HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT.

Sir,—lt is a great pity that such sarcastic and personal letters as the one signed by " One Interested," should appear in your valuable paper. I fail to see what bene- fit anyone gets by throwing mud one at another. Cer- tainly it is not the proper way to enlist sympathy and support. I think that there is one thing in his letter which in the interest of the movement, ought to be contradicted at once, that is" that the meeting (held on the 26th Jan.), consisted chiefly ot mere lads, 12 to 15 years of age." It is true that there were some youths at the meeting (as there is at every meeting of the kind), but not the majority that your correspondent wishes the public to believe. I admire his courage and straightfor- wardness in stating that he is not an assistant himself, but takes an interest in the cause. Efe asks the question —" Is the Market going to be closed earlier? " What on earth has that to do with the early closing of shops, I s/aould like to know? But there is one thing in his letter, as to which I quite concur with him,and that is that is, that the early closing of shops have the preference of the half-holiday. There are but a few places in town that keep open after seven o'clock, and I think that if we could get all to close their establishments at seven o'clock the first four nights and eight on Friday,and thus secure a general early closing we should have done a good stroke of business—and then work for the half-holiday. I am thoroughly convinced that the above is by far the best course to take, and I beg to commend it to the notice of the new Association which has been formed, and which I hope will be sup- ported by us all. Apologizing for trespassing upon your valuable space. I am yours &c.,
SHOP ASSISTANT.
OWN LIFE POLICIES.

Sir,—My only object in answering Mr.Moorfield's first letter was to dispute his statement that the use of " own life " policies for assurances on the life of another, was responsible for gambling. I said that as far as my experience went insurance gambling was not the result of the use of " own life " policies. In proof of this, I will give the mode of working adopted by a large office, which has only the " own life "policy form. Before a policy is issued the relationship between the proposer and the proposed and the proposer's interest in the life are ascertained. If the interest be insufficient, theproposal is promptly rejected, but when once ac- accepted the payer of the premuim, although he may not be the next of kin, need not fear that any person will be allowed to prevent him receiving the sum assured. It is invariably paid to the proposer, whose name is well known at the office.

Notwithstanding all this, I, like Mr. Moorfield, think it would be better if every Company put on the face of the policy the name of the person in whose interest it had been granted. The legal position of the paver would then be beyond question. If this were done, however, a man would still be able to assure his parents, brothers, sisters, Stc., if he could only show that their death would be to him an expense. Business of this sort was until recently, and I believe still is, readily accepted by the Company Mr. Moorfield is proud to represent, and by many other Companies, which use the " life of another" form.

In conclusion, let me inform Mr. Mocrfield that I am not an" important official of an important office in the town ;" neither am I the champion of " own life " pro- posals. I merely deny that they encourage or cause gambling. And, further, let me say that I have neither the inclination nor the time to continue the contro- versy.—Yours truly.
HENRY H. DUTTON. With this letter, the correspondence on this subject is closed for the present.—ED. Ex.]
A WORKING-MAYS QUESTION.

see from the Queen's Speech that a bill to amend the Employer's Liability Act, 1880, is to be raised to life again in the coming Session of Parliament. The object of the bill is to orohibit workmen from contract- ing out of the provisions of the Act. Two bills have been previously brought into the House of Commons having the same object : one by Mr. Burt and the other by Mr. A. O'Connor, in 1886, but neither came to any- thing as there was a change of Government. The pre- sent Government thereupon took charge of the bills,pro- mising to bring them into the House in an amended form. Mr. Burt's bill originally allowed contracts to stand good if made before the passing of the bill, and no appeal to a higher court would be allowed without con- sent, except the amount claimed exceeded £lOO, while Mr. O'Connor places the limit at £2OO. In the commit- tee stages of these twin bills, it was agreed to allow con- tracts out of the bill, if an equivalent' to the bill was given and a guarantee of the payment of the sum as- sured, providing that the Board of Trade was satiafied with the agreement. lam informed that in one tirge company's works there have been about 170 accidents in twelve months.and not one cf these would have come within the sphere of the Act, and yet all these have been benefitted by the contract which exists netween em- ployers and their workmen. Personally, 1 know one man who had his leg broken in the street, returning home at night, and another in crossing the Lancashire and Yorkshire line at Wigan while going home who was killed, and both these cases were attended to by the con- tract. All these cases were outside the scope of the Act, so that if contract was forbidden, not one penny wouid have been received to relieve the distfess caused by these accidents. Mr. Broadhurst's name appears on the hack of Mr. Burt's bill, and he seems very sore with the Government for their reference to the hill in the Speech from the Throne. Now, sir, if the option of contract is stopped, the Act will lose more than half its value to the workmen of this country. In ten years the sum of £32,000 has been claimed under the Act in the law courts, but only £15,000 has been obtained,and out of that the lawyer's fees (no small item), are to be deducted before the working-men get a penny of the sum due to them. I see, according to the annual report of the L. and N.W.R. Co., that out of their insurance society the sum of £29,239 18s. 7d. has been paid an account of accidents, and of that sum £15,169 6s. id., has been contributed by the Company itself, which with the sum contributed to the Running Depart- ment will amount to the total of about £20,000" Sir, I think it will not take much stretch of thought to discern which is best for the workiag-men. The Act is quite necessary to make some employers more careful to nrotecttheir workmen, but where a contract satisfac- torily secures botta safety and immense benefits to the rnen, why not Jet such contracts still stand as legal ? Yours truly, A WORKING-MAN.

div.head: Earlestown. Feb. 15th.
div.p: Earlestown. Feb. 15th.
A LABOUR BUREAU FOR WARRINGTON.
Sir,—ln the course of a conversation with you res- pecting the adVAncetnent of Warrington, you were good enough to ask me to write you it letter upon the founda- tion of a labour bureau in this town.

The object and wee of Audi a bureau, would no doubt commend itself to all when familiar with its working. To put the matter as plainly and as briefly as, possible, there are a large number of persons in this town seeking .evnployment ; there are a large number of manufac- turers, employers of labour, and others requiring skilled labour and hired help. The plan adopted by persons out of situations in this town is to call round upon the manufacturers at their factories and offer their help. When the manufacturer or employer of labour requires assistance, at that moment the labourer in all probabi- lity is not to be found.

A labour bureau is intended to meet the want of both sections of the coniniunity in regard to the question of supply and demand of labour. At that bureau persons seeking employment enter their names under the vari- ous classifications for which they are qualified, brick- layers, tua.sons, joiners, carpenters, blacksmiths, fitters, kc., whilst in those towns where there are stap`e trades : the different artificers in their specified departments of each trade are carefully noted. In the same way the different industries conducted in a town are also set :Orin, contractors, soals-naakers, borax manufacturer!, I

brush manufacturers, Wire weavers, iron manufacturers, tanners, glue and gelatine manufacturers, brewers, tool manufacturers, &c. The master or manufacturer requir- ing help, whether for a long or short period has conse- quently only to send to the labour bureau to get any description of labour he requires, whilst those out of employment find a concentrated source of information as to the prospect of their finding employment, without wasting their time and energy, as well as occupying the time of others in their fruitless endeavours to get work. The intelligence department could also supply the in- formation as to what class of labour was in most re- quest, and what demand there was for any special class of labour in any other town throughout the country. The want of such an organisation as this in Warring- ton would perhaps be more readily recognised if it were generally known tkat it has the most manufactories of any town of its size in the United Kingdom. There being no less than tweaty-eight different industries car- ried on in the tow, and neighbourhood. This fact clearly shows that Warrington enjoys advantages of one sort or another that are recognised to a more or less extent by the manufacturing community, and with the advent of the Manchester Ship Canal it does not require a far- sighted person to foretell that within a very brief period the population of Warrington must increase much more rapidly than it has done in the past, and probably more than any other town in the United Kingdom. Apart from the desirability of establishing a bureau of information for those coming to the town in search of employment, or the assistance of manufacturers locating here in the near future, and who require labour in the pursuit of their enterprises, the question is whether or not such a bureau would of benefit to the town. The next question that naturally arises is what is it going to cost, who is going to work it, and what is there in it? The cost would be very light and would consist of an office and a set of books As to who should work it, it is an open question whether the bureau should be con- ducted by private enterprise, which is frequently done, or under municipal authority. The fees payable in the event of an engagement would snore than recoup the outlay of expenditure. The labour bureau is no new idea : it is an institution in almost every town in the United States of America, and elsewhere, whilst in this country we have Registry Offices for domestic servants, and Clerks' Associations. These institutions pay well, and are extensively patron- ized, and there is no doubt that if the labour bureau were established in Warrington it would in a very short time meet with the success that it deserves, and confer a boon upon the inhabitants at large.—l have the honour to be your obedient servant, E. L. FLEMING. Dial Mill, Warrington, Feb. 15th, 1892.

div.head: WORD TO WORKING-MEN.
div.p: A WORD TO WORKING-MEN.

Sir,—ln my last letter published in your issue of Jan. 30th, I pointed out that the Trades Congress in September last passed a reqolution to make the payment of members of Parliament a test question at the next general election, which was carried by 169 against 9 votes. This is an encouraging sign of the times. Working-men are emerg- ing from sleep and mere party politics. It is high time that we as working-men were alive to our own interests, and forsook for ever that political side which still opposes almost every good measure hitherto justly re- quired by the working-classes of this century. What a thoughtless and suicidal act for any working-man to vote for any Tory candidate, or Liberal candidate, who sets himself, as Mr. Robert Pierpoint has already done, directly against the resolution of the Trades Congress with reference to payment of members, &c! And why should any werking-man continue to vote Tory or Liberal simply because his father did ? Such folly is only equalled by refusing to live civilised lives, because our ancestors were originally savages, and knew not any better way of living, arc. My fellow working-men, have more Mbral courage! Think for yourselves ! Act like men! Bo no longer mere tools.

Direct Representation.—Why should we be denied this equitable reform longer ? Almost every other civilised nation now pay all their Legislators, thus rendering it easy for the working classes to send men who person- ally know all the needs, sufferings, and hardships of the toiling masses, which, indeed, the rich rulers know next to nothing about and ,the bulk of them care less about. Our brethren in the colonies now pay M.P.'s. New Zealrnd, Canada, and Victoria pay from £250 to £4OO per annum. The United States award their representatives £1,041 yearly, with railway fair of 20 cents, per mile. Franc( gives £.365 yearly. Even Por- tugal pays LIEST a year, while Belgium awards £lB 15s. ,per month as long as the chambc.r is sitting, and poor Greece pays £2O motithly, while Denmark allows 15s. per day, Norway awards 15s. 4d. per day during the sitting of the House. Switzerland pays 10s. a day, Prussia 9s. per day, and Austria 20s. daily. Sweden awards £lB 145., and also travelling expenses, for the session of four months, and very justly inflicts a fine on its members of 10 rix-dollars (11s.) for every day's non-attendance. Anciently in England, an Act waspassed in 1541, involving any member in the loss of his wages who left the House of Commons without the Speaker's consent before the end of the session. Had tiois been still in force, Sir Gilbert Greenall would have been fined for non-attendancs, unless the utterly selfish act of being present once, and voting for the Brewers' and Publicans' Compensation Bill had prevented so just a retribution falling to his lot. Where is the justice that the so-called upper and middle classes should have 667 out of 670 to legislate in their interest—in the interest of those of whom John Ruskin soundly and fittingly says "Nearly every pro- blem of State policy, and economy, as at present under- stood and practised,consists in some device for persuad- ing you labourers to go and dig up dinner for us reflec- tive and testhetical persons, who like to sit still, and think, or admire, so that when we get to the bottom of the matter. We find the inhabitants of this earth broadly divided into two great masses •, the present paymasters spade in hand, original and imperial producers of turnips ; and, waiting on them all ropnd, a crowd of polite persons, modestly expectant of turnips, for some too often, theoretical service." Now why i 3 this state of things to be perpetuated for ever? Wny should the real producet of wealth, he who wrings it from the earth either by tillage or by mining, be the poorest man in the community? ..

flow' is property to be more equally and happily divided ? Why should we as "dumb driven cattle" allow such men to have all the law-making in their own I hands, for their selfish ends? Are we not already taxed too heavily, and paid too little for our labour to be sad- dled with election expenses and pp ymPnt of working- men representatives, to the num ber,say, of 300 members, ; needful to cope with the other 370 M.P.'s ? Why, then, ' in future vote for such men as Mr. Robert Pierpoint, who have declared against State payment of M.P.'s in order to do their utmost to prevent us from stopping this grinding the faces of the poor, and freeing our noses from the grinding stone? As to the costs of paying all M.P.'s, we now pay the Cabinet • why not also pay the rest ? We pay the judges for administering the law. Why not pay those who make the law? Cut down the shameful pension list, abolish gory,inhuman wars,cease to glory in such cursed crimes against your fellow-man, and God. The cost of payment of members would thus be more than met, to the honour, glory, and all-abiding happiness of our dear old England. A WORKING-MAN. February 10th, 1892.

div.p: PENKETH.

311.TTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. The weedy meeting of the above association was held on Wednesday, in the schoolroom. There was a moderate attendance. Mr. Garnett occupied the chair. Toe last of the anonymous papers received by Mr. .Tones were read, and an interesting discus- sion followed. NEW LETTER DESPATCH FROM POST OFFICE. We understand that the Warrington Postmaster (Mr. C. H. Kerry) has made arrangements with the postmistress of the Penketh Post Office (Mrs. Clarke) for an additional despatch of letters from here. Final arrangements have not yet been made, hut letters which are required to be despatched by this mail should be posted by nine o'clock or a few minutes after at the latest. The change will come into operation on and after Monday next. BAND OF HOPE MEETING. The monthly public meeting of the above Band ,of Hope was held lsst evening week, in the Wee_ leyan schoolroom. There was a fair attendance. Mr. William Roberts, of Warrington, occupied the chair. An excellent, programme, consisting of songs ,r and recitations, was contributed by the choir and elder scholars in a most praiseworthy manner, and was much appreciated. In the course of a few re- marks, Mr. Roberts mentioned a number of incidents which had come under his personal notice, showing , the ill and terrible effects of free indulgence in in- toxicating liquors. He Anted the friends to sign the pledge, and to always avoid touching or tast- ing alcohol. Mr. Roberts's remarks were attentively • listened to. Mr. Roberts also offered for competition at the next meeting two prizes for the two hest re- citations given by the children. At the conclusion I of the programme, a hearty vote of thanks was ac- corded to Mr. Roberts for his services in the chair. and also to the choir and reciter s for their pleasant I entertainment. A collection was taken at the door ' in aid of the Band of [lope funds. Miss Garnett ac- companied the pieces on the piano in an able manner.
Thomas Leece. a Liverpool clerk, shlt himself on Tues- day morning. He had been suffering from depression, and said he would nut go to his office as he was no use there.

THE EX A )11N BRIMSTOOAN AN"fRAYCLE. (MIXED.) Bi Tum o' Dic o' Bon's. There's nobbut one remerkable thing happened this week, an' thad is Stead's bin lecturin' i' Man- chester on "The Church in Manchester," an'" The Churches and the general election," an' he hesn'd puffed General Booth, nor blaggarded Sir Charles Dilke ! When aw mention as aw'm referrin' to th' " Review o' Reviews" Stead,lots o' fooak 'II reviews to believe id, becose W. T.'s bin as full o' Sir Charles as another crank o' th name o' Mr. Dick were full o' King Charles an' his heyd. Stead's lectures bed plenty o' meyt in 'em, but aw'm rayther feard id'll be too strong for =oast as were theere, an' too Indigestible for others; their stummicks hes getten used to cooarser stuff, an' id wod tek twenty Steads to weean 'em. But there's nobbut one. After mentionin' as th' motto" No Scoundrel need apply" should be put up o'er tie doors o' th' Constituencies through which a chap passed to th' lleawse o' Com- mons, he sketched a programme as included sich items as " The Direct veto, Sunday closing, deal- ing with the opium traffic, temperance teaching, a closer union with the American Republic with a view to arbitration in international disputes, the evacuation of Egypt as soon as the work which we had undertaken there was thoroughly accomplished, and an honest dealing with labour questions." Aw say " ditto," to th' biggest pert o' th' items, an' to wod he said abeawt th' Church nod meddlin' wi' wod id dudn'd understand. Aw'm nod sure as th' Church could do so mich good in preychin' di' principle o' arbitration i' th' case o' strikes an' disputes. or bi' tekkin' up th' question o' th' law relatin' to women. The question is why doesn'd Stead set up as a payson, or a M.P ? Both owt to have a vacancy for a lost mate i' th' army, or a pilot ; but surely there's a constituency somewheere wi' a door as hes thad motto painted o'er id abeawt no sceawn- drel needin' to apply ! * *

Speykin' o' th' General, aw see he's settlin' deawn fro' his eawt ; he were tellin"em last Tuesda' fleet at Exeter Ho' as Ostrilia an' India formed a" mag- nificent inheritance." Th' hofe o' their advantages hedn'd bin towd ; th' success ill' three countries as he'd visited bed bin "marvellous ;" ten year sin' they hedn'd a single sowjer theere, but neaw aw suppooase they've a tooathri wed uns among th' 25,000, to say nowt o' th' two theawsand two bun- derd officers. Another thing he towd 'em wor as they bed a querter ov a million peawnds woth o' property. Aw'm sorry to hear this! But for o' thad id may grow an' grow till id rey- ches a full million—happen moore, an' they'll hey a. lively time on id when somebody else begins tawkin' abeawt chsendowin' th' Army, an' riflin' their barracks. div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO A. GIRL AT
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO A. GIRL AT
WESTON POINT.

--- Yesterday afternoon, Amy Bibby, a girl 12 years of age, daughter of Henry Hibby, of Clarke's-road, Weston Point, met with a terrible accident. She was picking cinders at the Salt Works, when she was knocked down by an engine and run over. Both her legs were taken off at the thighs, and Dr. McDougall said she could not possibly live many hours.

div.head: TUNNEL UNDER THE 3IERSEY.
div.p: THE TUNNEL UNDER THE 3IERSEY.
ANOTHER MISHAP.

Ni,e understand that the works in connection with the Vyrnwy aqueduct tunnel under the river Mersey, at Fiddler's Ferry, for the Liverpool Cor- poration Water Committee, were again brought to an abrupt standstill on Wednesday night by the giving way of the river bed and the consequent inrush of water which reached the air cham- ber. Fortunately, no lives were lost, although, owing to the sudden and unexpected na- ture of • the accident, the gang of tnen who were working at the time had great difficulty in getting up the shaft before the water was upon them. At the time when the accident occurred the total.length driven from the centre of the Lanca- shire shaft was nearly 600 ft., and the present contractors have, we believe, about reached the troublesome strata of sand which baffled and caused Messrs. Monk arid Newell 80 much difficulty. At the present time efforts are being made to repair the breach by throwing in large quantities of clay, and when this has been stir:ems:dully-- accomplished. the water will be pumped out of the tunnel and work resumed as soon as possible.
