div.head: TURDAN, FEBRUARY 20, 1892.
div.p: TURDAN, FEBRUARY 20, 1892.
FREE EDUCATION AND SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Steele. Runcorn School Board, summoned the following parents for not sending their children regularly to school :—Thomas Sharkey.. Mitt-street; Patrick Kilkenny, Fryer-street ; Michaeli Phillips, Mersey-street ; Thomas Millington, Cartwright- street; Thomas Woodflne, Mitt-street ; John Antrobus; Porter-street William Ellis, Zions Place ; Edward: Wilkinson, Windmill-street; John Bagley, Mill Brow (2 cases) ; William Price, Nelson-street (2 cases) ; Thomai Hughes. Briscoe-street; James Hughes. Stonehills ; Henry Snape, Gilbert-street ; William Martin, Brickkiln Houses (3 cases) ; Annie Nash, Nelson-street (2 cases) : Annie Dutton, Porter-street. The evidence of Visitor Bowyer showed that the defendants,with few exceptions, ' were old offenders. In reply to the Bench Mr. Bowyer ,said there had been no improvement in the attendance since the introduction of Free Education.—Mr. Reynolds I Said these were the worst lot of cases he had ever had before him. The cry formerly was that they had not the pence, but it had turned out as he expected. The children did not attend when the pence were provided. Each defendant was fined ss, including costs.

div.head: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

On Wednesday night, a man named Win. Charles Hough, aged 28, residing at Higher Ince, a brakes- man in the employ of the London and North-West- ern Railway Co., had a fatal accident on the line at Frodsham. A luggage train was standing in the siding at the station there to allow a passenger train to pass. When a train is put into a siding the red lamps are reversed to white to show that it is not on the main line. The deceased omitted to turnthe lamps of the luggage train, and the driver of the passenger train, as it approached, supposed the for'mer was on the main line. He whistled,and Hough jumped down to reverse his lamp, and was knocked down 13.5 the passenger engine. The ex- press from Chester to Warrington was stopped at Frodsham and the poor man was brought to Warrington, and conveyed to the Infirmary, where he died on Thursday afternoon. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, opened an iuquest at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-st., yesterday morning, but merely took formal evidence to admit of a certificate for burial. The deceased's widow and Emily Dobson, nurse at the Infirmary were the witnesses. They both stated• that be could not tell in the Infirmary how the accident happened. The enquiry was adjourned till one o'clock on Tuesday.

div.head: WARRINGTON PERFECT THRIFT
div.p: WARRINGTON PERFECT THRIFT
BUILDING SOCIETY.

The .first public ballot and concert in connection with this society took place in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st., last evening. Mr. Thomas Morris presided, and there was a moderate attendance. The chairman in his opening remarks, said that what- ever scheme was inaugurated in the town which had thrift at the end of it had his support, and although he was chairman of a Permanent Building Society something like 17 or 18 years old, still he was not jealous of that new society, which was managed by men who were, he believed, worthy of all respect. lie referred with approval to the methods adopted by the society for guarding itself against losses, and added that, al- though the society had only been in existence about ten weeks it had 126 members, who held 266 shares, which when fully paid up would amount t0.£26,600. After the Chairman's address the concert was proceeded with. It included songs by Mr. Taylor ; Mrs.• Hodges, Miss F. M. Cavanagh, !Mr. F. J. Dell, and Mr. A. Cavanagh ; duet by Messrs. F. J. Dell and A. Cavanagh, and a trio by ' Miss Cavanagh, Mrs. Hodges, and Mr. F. J. Dell. Mr. W. Horsley also gave his popular lecture on " Every man his own landlord," which was follow- ed with evident interest by the audience. A ballot was afterwards taken and resulted in the drawing of number 101, which entitled the possessor of that number, Mary Ma6oll, to the use of .ClOO.

div.head: BANKING SCHOOL PENCE.
div.p: BANKING SCHOOL PENCE.

It does not seem to he generally known that the Post Office authorities are offering special facilities for encouraging the banking of the school pence set free by the assisted education measure. The plan may be carried out as follows: The Post Office supplies the school manager or teacher with stamp slips specially prepared for his use. Each slip bears the name of the school and a Buses for the name of the scholar. Envelopes similarly- are supplied for the safe keeping of the slips. A credit stock of stamps of any amount up to £5 is supplied to the manager or teacher by the neighbouring postmaster, to whom is given a guarantee by two householders, to hold the Postmaster-General harmless against any loss or misapprepriation. On the day on which the school pence used formerly to be paid the manager or teacher exchanges any pence brought by the children for stamps, and affixes the stamps to the slips, which the children take home as evidence to their parents of the payment of the pence. The slips can then be either kept by the parents or returned to the school until the next depositing day. At certain intervals, say every month or every quarter, as may be arranged, a clerk from the nearest post office attends at the school and receives all stamp slips which are filled up, opening accounts in the individual names of the children in tile Post Office Savings Bank, hi which they henceforth become depositors. The opening of such an account does not step the use of the slips. The school pence are week by week converted into stamps as before, and, when the post office clerk next attends, the amount of the slips which have been filled up since kis last visit is credited to the child's account, and the pro- cess recommences. Thus a parent regularly investing his child's school pence will have put more than a pound in his name in the Post Office Savings Bank by the end of the year. As soon as a pound has been thus depos- ited, interest at the rate of BJ. for the year begins to rue, and at the end of each calendar year any accrued interest is added to the principal and itself carries interest.
'e ndorse(

The plan is an admirable one for encouraging habits of thrift; and we commend it to the atten- tion of school managers in this district in the hope that they will take steps to bring it into operation.

div.head: ANNUAL DRINK BILL
div.p: THE ANNUAL DRINK BILL

Dr. Dawson Burns, on behalf of the United Kingdom Alliance, issues his latest annual survey of the national expenditure on drink. The total amount spent in in- toxicating drinks in the United Kingdom during 1891 was £141.250,000 sterling. This huge sum means an r.x,nditure of £3 153. per head, reckoning women and children as well as men, or £lB 153. for vach family of five persons. Comparing the amounts with those pre- sented alyear ago, we find al4 increase amounting this year to £1,750,080. In foreign and colonial spirits, in- deed, there has been a decline ;but this has been largely overbalanced by the inzrease in home-made spirits and 'in beer. In the two latter classes the rise has been respectively £1,333.778 and 1,129,869 ; in the two former the fall has been £591,654 and £146,778.

div.head: TWO CHILDREN STRANGLED IN LIVERPOOL
div.p: TWO CHILDREN STRANGLED IN LIVERPOOL

An inquest was held by the Liverpool coroner, on Wednesday, on the bodies of the two children, Henry and Catherine Lascelles, who were found dead in bed on Monday, at 54, Freelands-st., Kirkdale, with pieces of , rope round their throats. John Lascelles„ a guards' checker, father of the deceased, said his wife had been strange in her mind, and the neighbours deposed to see- ing her with a piece of rope in her hand. She had suffered from influenza. The jury found that the chil- dren were strangled by the mother. This, the coroner remarked, was a verdict of wilful murder. The woman lies in a prostrate condition in the hospital from self- inflicted injuries. The remains of the two children who died by their ' mother's hand on Monday, were buried on Thursday afternoon, at Longmore-lane Cemetery, Walton,without the slightest demonstration, and in the presence of only the few mourners—five in all—who assembled at the graveside.

Joseph Deakin was found frozen to death on Tuesday, lying in a field at the back of Abbey Church, Tewkes- bury. A Berlin telegram indicates that there is a probability of the German Emperor visiting the World's Fair at Chicago in 1893. The will of the late Right Hon. W. H. Smith was sworn for probate an the 10th inst. The personalty is sworn at £1,764,000. A committee of Philadelphia citizens has purchased at Buffalo 15 car loads of flour for shipment to Russia in aid of the sufferers from famine. A friend to sailors residing in Yorkshire, has offered to the Missions to Seamen A steamer valued at £3OO for the use of their chaplain on the Tees. Henry Keegan, a survivor of the Balaclava charge, died in Ifirvaingham on Tuesday. He has been in neces- sitous c reumstances for some time. The corn tnanding officers of the various Naval Artillery Volunteer Corps, on Monday morning, received an inti- mation from the %Vac Office that the Naval Volunteers will be welcomed as art addition to the existing forces of Submarine Mining Engineers at the various centres. Their existence as a separate force is definitely tabooed.

div.head: WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTOGRA- PHIC SOCIETY.
ANNUAL EXHIBITION OF VIEWS.

The filth annual exhibition of lantern slides, and Concert in connection with the Warrington Ama- teur Photographic Society, were given in the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance. Mr. W. Pierpoint, vice-president, took the place of Mr. T. J. Down, the president, in his absence. The Chairman said in the absence of Mr. Down, he had been asked to preside over that meeting that night, and lie was extremely sorry Mr. Down was not present, because as every member of the Photographic Society knew, Mr. Down had taken a very great interest in the society since its very formation, and he knew that if it had not been for a very important engagement, Mr. Down would have been there to take the chair. He would like to say with reference to the society that to- night they were trying first of all to do what they could to amuse them, and then perhaps to interest them all in the art of photography. The society was increas- ing rather rapidly, and he was very glad to say that it included among its members both ladies and gentlemen. It would be much better, he thought, if they had more lady members, but at all events they were very pleased indeed to have ladies at all among them. Now he should like to say as to the art of photography, that, as a great many of them had seen now for a great number of years, some of the examples, of course, of professional photographers were really very beautiful works of art, and some of the works of the amateurs—well they would not say much about them. At all events, he had come to the conclusion that however many plates amateurs might use, it had not, to his mind, at all the effect of interfering with the work of the professional photographer, because, although the amateur was fairly good in amateur work,—he believed there were many amateurs who in landscape work were fully equal to the best professionals—yet when they came to portraiture the results produced were such as, to his mind, to at once show that there was no fear that the occupation of the professional photographer would ever be interfered with by the amateur. The amateur was never satisfied with himself, but was always think- ing his last negative would be better than the one before. When he had taken one he would think he had got into the way of doing it, and that there was no difficulty about it; and he had felt that Way, but he had found that the more he knew or tried to know about photography the more he felt his utter ignorance of the whole process. The Warrington Photographic Society, the Chairman mentioned, contained 80 to 70 members, and is increasing at the rate a per- haps 10 per cent, per annum. A number of slides were subsequently exhibited, the photographs having been , executed by the following members :—Messrs. James Bodle, John Fairhurst, Patterson, J. Skelton, H. N. Houghton, J. Pritchard, Harding, A. W. Paul, Kirkny, Brown (Fenketh), J. Hallowa (Stockton Heath), J. W. Cavanagh, Wm. Parkinson, R. Grahame, Wm. Robinson (Frodsham), Thos. Mather, and Thos. Welsby, and Miss Harding. The views included a number of local landscape and street scenes, one of those being of Walking Day in Warrington, besides portraits of well- known Warringtonians, and views of the Isle of Man, Liverpool, Devonshire, Blackpool, Windermere, York Minster. &c.. and many of them were of the highest artistic excelleJce. The lantern was ably managed by Mr. H. N. Houghton. The concert, of which Mr. H. Bond had the management,comprised the following items, some of the performances winning considerable applause: —Solo pianoforte, " Tarantelle," Thai berg, Mrs. W. B Roberts • song, "Molly Bawn," S Lover, Mr. Alfred Cavanagh; duet, flute and piano; 2nd Divertimento in C, Op. 39.. Hayseder, Mr. Peers Brinaelow and Mrs. W. D. Roberts; song, "For all Eternity," Angelo Mareheroni, Mrs. Pearson; duet, flute and piano (air with variations, dedicated to Paganini), Mayseder, Mr. Peers Brimelow and Mrs. Roberts; song, "The Bee and the Song,' F. E. Weatherley, Mrs. Pearson; song, "Off to Philadelphia" B. Haynes. Mr. Alfred Cavanagh; pianoforte solo, Salon Walzer, Alfred R. Sutton, Mrs. Roberts. The national anthem, concluded the proceedings.

Lister presiding, charged with neglecting to meintain her child. She was convicted of this offence in September, last in her absence,and Mr. Lister then told the police not to execute the warrant if she kept away out of Lymm. On a navvyt with whom the prisoner cohabited, coming forward and saying he was going to marry her, the magistrates discharged her.

DEATH OF MR JOHN CHORLRY.—We regret to record the death of Mr. John Otiorley, a well-known rssident of Lvmin for nearly three-quarters of a century. He had been in failing health for more than 12 months. He was interred ou Tuesday, when a number of friends assembled to pay a last tribute of respect to one who had in his time been an active worker in the public interest. He took a prominent part in resisting the levying of the church rate, and was amongst those who brought the question to a crisis in Lymm. He was a Congregation- alist of a prenonnced type after he left the Wesleyan body. During his early manhood and prime he was one of the most jovial of men. lie was als a staunch Liberal all his life. He leaves a widow and only eon, now resid- ing at Oldham.

NEW Biu.s.—Bills were read a first time to provide for the registration of teachers ; to enable women to be elected and to serve on County Coiencils ; and to com- pensate agricultural tenants for all improvements.

Mr. David Thomas econded. The Attorney-General, defending the appoint- ment, said the selection seemed to be very popular. Mr. 0. Morgan, Sir J. Be did not wish to disfranchise the illiterate v,iter, but lie .leAir change should be made in the present system. div.head: SEVERE -WEATHER.
div.p: THE SEVERE -WEATHER.

BLOCK OF RAILWAY TRAINS. At Wareham, Dorset, the snow drifts are six feet deep. Twenty-five degrees of frost were registered at Locker- bie yesterday morning. Snow is falling at Taunton, and the drifts in the roads have nearly stopped all traffic. Accounts to hand yesterday morning show that there is no diminution of the severity of the weather through- out the kingdom. A Totnes telegram states that the snow in Devonshire is a foot deep, and is still falling. Some of the morning trains had not started.

The steamship 4Valter Raleigh was lost by a tug off Cape Clear in the gale, on Thursday riiht. The crew were saved by the tug. The vessel stated to be ashore between Dover and Folkstone is the Swansea barque Aberleinno. She is badly strained, and is leaking. At Bude, on North Cornwall coast, a blizzard has been blowing since five o'clock yesterday morning, and the roadways are blocked by snow, which has drifted to a great depth. Telegrams received from different parts of the coun- try indicate that the severe weather continues to be genend. A vessel stranded on Wednesday night during the snow storm, between Dover and Folkstone. Snow in Norfolk is eight inenes deep.

div.head: EVERTON VACANCY.
div.p: THE EVERTON VACANCY.
Mr. E.. 1. Willox, Conservative, was, on Monday, re- turned unopposed as the Parliamentary representative of the Everton Division, Liverpool, In the room of Mr. Whitley, deceased.
SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC AT BOMBAY.

BOMBAY, THURSDAY,—There is a serious epidemic of smallpox in Bombay. Twenty-three deaths from the disease occurred in this city during last week, and the malady continues to spread. There is a great emigra- tion going on from drought-stricken districts, the peopl., going with their cattle to the localities wilt re fodder and water are plentiful. Prices continue high.
THE LOSS OF THE TAHITI AND OVER
370 LIVES.

- • - --- A Sydney correspondent says that by the disaster to the Tahiti over 370 lives were lost. The majority of the unfortunate people were natives of the Gilbert Island, The Tahiti was a brigantine of 290 tons register, and was one of the fastest sailors in the South Sea Island trade. At the time of the disaster she was taking 370 islanders from the Gilbert Group to San Benito, Mexico, to work on the coffee plantations under a three years' agreement.

WHALLEY'S' "DIDDLING CHAIR." At the sale on Tuesday of the fornlture of the Black- burn office of Whalley, the solicitor, whose gigantic frauds have caused widespread distress,uproarious mirth was caused by the sale of Whalley's "diddling chair," so dubbed because the defunct lawyer invariably seated therein the victims he was desirous of overreaching. The chair, which was of oak, of antique pattern, was knocked down amidst cheers for 10s. to a gentleman, who was asked to present it to the Blackburn Museum.
THE DAISY HOPKINS CASE.
A CONTRADICTION.

In reference to a report, which appeared on Wednes- day, that a young woman who gave the name of Daisy Hopkins was sent tr) prison for seven days, at the Lon- don Mansion House, for being drunk and disorderly, the solicitor acting on behalf of Daisy Hopkins in the Cam- bridge Spinning House case states that his client has not left Cambridge for a week, and that his clerk saw her on Wednesday afternoon, at her home at Cambridge.

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN LONDON.

A fire, which at one time assumed very threatening proportions, broke out early on Thursday morning in the large block of buildings in Gray's Inn-road, London, occupied by Messrs. Sage and Co., shoptitters. A build- ing of three storeys was completed gutted, and the adjoining shops and h•iuses were seriously damaged. No less than thirty engines were at one time at work r,n the flames and protecting the surrounding property, much of which is occupied as dwellings by people of the work- ing class.

The inland coal porters of London resumed work on Monday morning, but the " sea-borne " workers are still in open revolt. 'I lie aspect of affairs is still very serious, and dissension continves to prevail among the former leaders of the men.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. RUNCORN NORTH ELECTORAL DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Your District Liberal Association having unanimously asked me to offer myself as Candidate at the forthcoming Election, I have great pleasure in doing se, and trust that by your good will and active assistance I may have the honour of representing my native town in our County Parliament. TI 11 am returned as your Member I shall endeavour on all occas- ions to watch over and promote the Interests of this division, and as a man of business keep a watchful eye on the expendi- ture of the County Rates. I shall also givemry earnest attention to the administration of the varied business under the control of the Council, and trust that if elected my attendance and action may show that your confidence in me as your representative has not been misplaced. It is difficult, within the limits of an ordinary advertise- ment,to refer to ail the questions coming or likely to oome under the notice of the Council, but I hope before the day erf Election to have several opportunities of a more extended reference to them and also the pleasure of making your personal acquaintence. Faithf ally yours, WILLIAM OCKLESTON. Halton-road. liisncorn. February 18th. 1892.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OP THE RUNCORN /TORTH ELECTORAL DIVISION. LIDIES I.YD OTNTLEMEN,— Three years ago you honoured me by electing arts your Representative on the County Council, and I venture again to appeal to you for your votes and interest at the ap proaching Election. I solicit yeur support on the same lines as I did previously —as an Independent Candidate—believing that the business of the Council it best conducted without the introduction of I Politics and my constant aim has been to serve the Division without respect-to Party. If elected I hope to pursue in the future the same policy. I am strongly In favour of the proposed roadway across the Mersey, believing it will considerably benefit both Counties. Any measure having in view the adoption and maintenance of all main roads as county roads shall have my careful con- sideration and support. Technical Education shall have my best attention, but I feel that the disposalut the grants will want careful attention. Shoult, it be your pleasure to again elect me I win do my utmost to protect yoar interests and advance the prosperity of this important Division. lam, Ltdies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, C. W. HAZLEZIURST, Runcorn. Fehroms, 18th, 1892.

C HESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH DIVISION OF RUNCORN. LADIF.9 AND GENTLEMEN, Three years ago you did me the .honour of return ing me as your first representative in the Cheshire County Council. Having endeavonredto serve you diligently and faithfully during that period, I venture a gain to ask for your renewed confidence and support. It is impossible, within the limits of a brief address, to deal with the various matters which have engaged the atten- tion of the Coundil, but I may be permitted to refer to one or two which more immediately concern the town andseigh- bourhood of Runcorn. By the CUBtOMS and Excise Act, 1889, a large sum of money was placed at the disposal of the Council for the purposes of Technical and Mtnual Instruction. As a member of the committee charged with the distribution ef that fund, I have endeavoured to utilise it to the best advantage, in providing efficient commercial and technical Instruction for all classes' ot the corn. unity. 'An annual grant of £220 has already been made to the Runcorn Improvetr ent Commissioners by the County Council, and I would use my best endeavours to obtain from the same source a substantial grant towards the erection of a Technicol Institute in Runcorn, so that :the town may possess a w tally building in which to carry on -its educational operations. The question of the County roads has also rezelved my attention, and it is gratifying to know that there is every probabilityof the main road leading from Haltou boundary to Humorn Railway Station being at an early date either Wien over by the County Council or made the subject of an anisnal grant by the Conseil, either of which would mean a saClng to the ratepayers of Runcorn of about £2OO per annum.. At tho last meeting of the Council a resolution. which I bad the honour to move, was•CArried appointing a committee to repott upon the question-ref vital importance to R unoorn— of a vehicular bridge across the Mersey, connecting the towns of Runcorn and Widnes, thus affording a valuable' means of inter-communfeation between the Counties of Lau cashire and Cheshire. This scheme has my heartiest sup- port, and no effort on my part •would be wanting to make the desired means of eommustistion an accomplished fact. In thus appealing for your ;suffrages, I do so on purely independent lines. I seek tc enter the Council untram- melled by ties of party or seat, and if returned I shall con- sider all quections, from whenceiend by whom introduced, from the single standpoint a an independent ratepayer, onslous only Co secure the happizess and well-being of his fiellow.citizens. and the industrial and commercial proa- Nifty of the Cvnnty in which their it is cast. I have the honour to remain. Ladies and Gentlemen, Your faitlatrel Servant, PILEUP SPEAKMAN. Wbc7donnt. Higher Runcorn, February Mb, 1892.

LOSS OF A WHALER AND 18 LIVES. NEW YORK, TRURSDAY.—The whaling boat Tamerlane, belonging to Hawaii, was lost on the 2nd inst., the cap- tain and seventeen of the crew being drowned. THE PRINCE OF WALES AND SIR HENRY JAMES. It is notified in last night's "Gazette" that the Prince of Wales has appointed Sir Henry James, M.P., to be Attorney General to his Royal Highness, vice Sir Charles Hull appointed Recorder of London. THE COMING GENERAL ELECTION. In nearly all quarters it is agreed that Thursday night's proceedings in the House of Commons have strengthened the Impression that a dissolution may be looked for at or soon after Easter. The " Times," in its Political Notes, says :—After Mr. Balfour's explanation. of the provisions of the Irish Local Government Bill, conversation in the lobby turned mainly upon the pos- sibilities of the measure being passed before the dissdlu- tion. MYSTERIOUS TRAGEDY IN BOLTON. SUPPOSED ATTEMPTED OUTRAGE AND MURDER. A profound sensation was created in Bolton on Thurs- day night by the discovery at a late hour of a woman lying in a back street in a semi-conscious condition, with her throat fearfully gashed, and bearing every evidence of a fearful struggle. A man's hat was found near her body, and an open clasp-knife in another part of the street. She was taken to tee infirmary, where she managed to gasp out, "a man did it," and then relapsed into unconsciousness. Yesterday the victim as identified. She is a married woman named Elizabeth Mather, but has been cohabit- ing with a man named James Whitely, whom she has implicated. He is in custody. Her depositions have been taken, and she is not expected to recover. Whitely will be brought before the magistiates to-day (Satur- day.)
